activity: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
knowledge_domain: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
fact: The 'Concorde fallacy' is named after the British and French governments continuing to fund the Concorde airliner after they recognized there was no longer an economic case for it.
story:
Coralie laid the two envelopes on her duvet side by side, the way she'd seen her mother lay out fabric before cutting. One was thin, a single sheet from the conservatory. The other held the deposit slip for the summer at Mr. Castillo's studio, three afternoons a week assisting with the little kids' painting classes, and the money was real money, the first she would ever have earned.

"They're not the same kind of thing," she said to the room, because Francis and Izaak were in it, cross-legged on the rug with the last of the pretzels.

Francis looked up from his phone. "Then don't compare them."

"She's comparing them," Izaak said. "That's the whole problem."

The conservatory letter said the intensive ran six weeks, all of July and half of August, with a recital on the fourteenth. The studio slip said June through August, Tuesdays, Wednesdays, Thursdays. She had done the calendar math so many times the numbers felt soft. Overlap didn't matter; even without a single conflicting date, she could not do both and keep her grades, and the grades were the thing her father called non-negotiable, though he said it gently, the way people say things they've already decided.

"I keep thinking," she said, "that if I turn down the conservatory it proves I was never serious about it."

"That's not what it proves," Izaak said.

"You don't know what it proves. Neither do I."

Francis rolled onto his back. He had come straight from the pool where he lifeguarded, hair still damp, and his voice had gone flat. "I put in for more hours."

"You hate that job," Coralie said.

"I bought the uniform." He said it like a closing argument. "Sixty bucks. whistle, the shirt, the certification course, all of it. If I quit now, the sixty bucks was for nothing."

Izaak sat forward. "That's the Concorde fallacy."

"The what?"

"The Concorde fallacy. The British and French governments kept funding the Concorde airliner even after they knew there was no economic case for it anymore. They'd already spent so much that stopping felt like losing more." He was picking pretzel salt off his knee, not looking at anyone. "My sister did a paper on it. The money's gone either way, Francis. It doesn't come back because you suffer more."

"I'm not suffering," Francis said, but he said it quietly, and pulled his collar up though the room wasn't cold.

Coralie turned the studio slip over. On the back, in Mr. Castillo's cramped hand, was a note he'd added when she'd gone to ask about the job: Your eye is better than your patience. That can be fixed. She had read it as flattery at first. Now she read it again and thought it might be a diagnosis. The conservatory wanted her patience; the studio wanted her eye; her father wanted her transcripts; and she could purchase exactly one of these futures with her one summer, and the others would go dark, quietly, the way a shop closes.

"So which one am I throwing good money after?" she asked.

"Neither," Izaak said. "You haven't spent anything yet. That's the thing. Francis already lost his sixty dollars. You haven't lost anything except sleep."

"That's worse," she said. "At least he has a fallacy. I just have two envelopes."

Francis laughed, a short surprised sound, and then sat up. "Okay, wait. Honest question. If you had to pick right now. No thinking."

She looked at the envelopes. The conservatory letter had arrived first and she had wanted it longer, and she understood suddenly that wanting-it-longer was its own kind of sunk cost, a reason that was not a reason, and she refused to equivocate with herself about that the way she'd been doing for eleven days.

"I'd pick the studio," she said. "I think. Because of the kids, and the money, and because I could still practice at night." She heard herself stacking qualifiers and stopped. "No. I'd pick the studio."

"You don't sound sure," Francis said.

"I'm not sure. I'm decided. Those aren't the same."

She picked up the conservatory envelope and put it in the drawer of her nightstand, not the trash, and the soft sound of the drawer closing made the choice feel physical, a door weight on its hinges. Then she texted Mr. Castillo, typed and deleted the apology she'd drafted in her head, and sent only the plain sentence: I'd like to take the job, if it's still open.

"Sixty dollars," Francis said, to no one. He was looking at his phone, at the pool schedule probably, his jaw set in that sullen line his face took whenever anyone cornered him. Then he opened another app, and Coralie saw it was a job board, listings scrolling under his thumb, and he angled the screen away as if she might grade him on it.

Izaak reached over and took the last pretzel.

Her phone buzzed on the duvet. Mr. Castillo: Tuesday, then. Bring your own brushes.

She held the phone against her chest for a second, then set it face down between the envelopes' empty spaces, one rectangle of warmth on the empty bed.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Food-safety guidance says refrigerated food must be kept at or below 4 degrees Celsius (40 degrees Fahrenheit) to slow the growth of bacteria.
story:
Jaxon woke to sun through the diaphanous curtains his mother had hung the year before, thin enough that the backyard came through them like a watercolor. He lay still for a moment, listening. The house was quiet in a way that meant she was already up, already moving, already pretending this Saturday was like any other. In the kitchen she was scraping the last of the butter onto toast and not meeting his eyes. He ate quickly, took the bus route he'd memorized twice, and got to the food bank ten minutes early, which was also a kind of pretending, since his shift didn't start for another forty.

The warehouse smelled of cardboard and cold. Andres was already there, stacking cans with the ruthless efficiency of someone who treated volunteering like a sport, and Zoe sat at the intake table with a clipboard, twisting her pen. Ms. Fischer, who ran the place, handed Jaxon a hairnet and a pair of gloves and said, "You're on sorting. Follow Andres." That was the whole orientation.

He worked through the morning crate by crate. Dented beans, dented tomatoes, a bag of rice with a hole someone had taped over. It was easy work, almost soothing, and he let himself think he might actually be good at this, that the hours would go down on a sheet somewhere and mean something. Around eleven, Zoe came looking pale.

"There's milk," she said. "On the dock. It's been sitting out there, I don't know how long."

Andres wiped his hands. "Donations came in at eight. So three hours."

Jaxon followed them out. The loading dock was a concrete lip open to the June heat, and beside the shuttered door sat a crate of gallon jugs, plastic sweating in the sun. He picked one up. It wasn't cold at all. It was the temperature of the air, of the pavement, of his own hands.

"Somebody should have put it away," Andres said. "Who signed for it?"

Zoe checked her clipboard. The line for received-by was blank. Jaxon felt something tighten in his chest, a suspicion he didn't yet have the shape of, and he turned the jug over looking for the sticker. Most of the food bank's dairy came from a supermarket chain that slapped blue labels on everything. These jugs had no labels at all. They had been carried in by hand, that was clear enough, in a soft-sided cooler bag that now lay collapsed beside the crate.

He found Ms. Fischer in the walk-in. "The milk on the dock," he said. "How do we know if it's still okay?"

She pointed at a laminated chart taped to the doorframe, the kind with cartoons on it, and went back to her inventory sheet. He read it twice. Refrigerated food must be kept at or below 4 degrees Celsius, 40 degrees Fahrenheit, to slow the growth of bacteria. The walk-in thermometer said 2. The dock, in the sun, was another world entirely. He carried the chart back outside with him and held it up for Zoe and Andres.

"Anything above that, it's out," he said. "It sat at dock temperature for three hours. There's no thermometer reading low enough to save it."

"That's like thirty gallons," Andres said. "That's real money."

Zoe looked at the crate, then at the cooler bag, then at her blank clipboard, and Jaxon understood she was doing the same arithmetic he was. Unlabeled. Hand-delivered. This morning. He had watched his mother carry a soft-sided cooler bag to the bus stop at seven-fifteen, and she hadn't said where she was going, and he had asked nothing because he was afraid of the answer. He had told her he was volunteering. She had told him she had errands.

"It's hers," he said quietly, before he could decide not to. "I think it's ours. From our fridge. We bought too much. There was a coupon." It came out wrong, all of it, the way the truth does when you've been keeping it folded up small.

Zoe's face didn't change the way he expected. "People donate from their own kitchens all the time," she said. "That's not the problem. The problem is it sat in the sun."

Andres crouched and pulled a jug from the bottom of the crate, out of the shade of the top layer, and pressed his palm against the plastic. "Bottom ones might be cooler. Jaxon, is there a thermometer that isn't for the walk-in?" There was, in the office, a probe thermometer in a drawer, and Jaxon went to get it slowly, giving himself the length of the hallway to think. He had come here this morning wanting the hours to be simple, wanting to hand out cans to strangers and feel clean about it. Instead the morning had problematized everything he'd planned to feel. If the milk was his family's, then throwing it out was both the right call and a strange kind of mercy, his mother spared from ever knowing her donation had gone wrong. If it wasn't hers, then somewhere a neighbor was driving home proud of herself, and the milk was still garbage.

He tested the bottom jugs first. Nineteen degrees. Then the shadiest corner of the crate. Sixteen. Nothing anywhere close to four, nowhere near forty Fahrenheit. He carried the crate to the waste area himself, jug by jug, and Zoe held the lid for him, and neither of them said anything consoling. When it was done, she wrote a note on the intake sheet in the received-by line: left on dock, discarded per temperature guidance.

His mother would be home by now, probably unpacking other errands, real or invented. Jaxon pulled off his gloves and looked at the empty space on the concrete where the crate had been. He took out his phone and typed, Did you go by the food bank today? Then he stood there a long moment with his thumb over send.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: Before DNA can be copied, the enzyme helicase unwinds the double helix by breaking the hydrogen bonds that hold the base pairs together.
story:
The waiting room smelled like antiseptic and damp fur, and Jordyn spread her flashcards across two plastic chairs while a tabby in a carrier yowled at her elbow. Monday's biology exam covered transcription and translation, and she had promised Ms. Costa, whose clinic she shadowed on Saturdays, that she would know it cold by now. She did not know it cold. She knew that DNA made RNA made protein, the way she knew that Paris was the capital of France, which was to say she could recite it and picture nothing.

Daven pushed through the door with his bike helmet still on, holding a shoebox with holes punched in the top. Inside was a garter snake he'd found half-frozen behind the school greenhouse, and he'd carried it four blocks because Jordyn worked here, or near here, and he trusted her to know what to do. She didn't. She was seventeen and unpaid and mostly filled water bowls.

"Ms. Costa's in surgery until noon," Jordyn said. "A dog ate a sock."

"Can you just look at him?" Daven set the box beside her flashcards. "You know animal stuff."

"I know how to fold towels." But she picked up the box anyway, because it was warmer than arguing, and carried it past the kennels to the exam room where the reptile heater sat under a towel. The snake coiled listlessly toward the warmth, and Daven stood with his hands jammed in his pockets like he was the one who'd been debilitated by the cold.

She went back for her cards, and when she returned he'd picked up the top one and was squinting at it. "What even is this?"

"Study stuff. Exam Monday." She took the card from him, then put it face down, embarrassed by how little the word on it had meant to her an hour ago.

"Read me one," Daven said. "I'll quiz you. You're quizzing me on whether he's alive every five minutes, so fair trade."

She read the question about the first step, the unzipping, and before she could recite her memorized answer, Daven pulled down the zipper of his jacket, all the way, so the two halves fell open over his T-shirt. "Okay, so like that. My bio teacher last year did this exact move." He held the separated halves apart. "The enzyme's called helicase, and it unwinds the double helix by breaking the hydrogen bonds between the base pairs. That's the whole thing. Zipper open."

Jordyn looked at the jacket, then at the snake, then at the jacket again. Something reorganized itself in her head, the way a drawer does when you finally stop forcing it and lift it out at the correct angle. "So it's a zipper," she said slowly. "Not a copy machine. I kept picturing a photocopier making a duplicate of the whole document at once, and that's why the rest wouldn't stick."

"What rest?"

"The parts after. The message getting read out and turned into protein." She shuffled through the cards, laying them along the exam table's edge in a line: unzip, read one strand, build the RNA letter by letter, send that message out, then the ribosome reading it in threes and snapping amino acids together. A protein, assembled like the sentence it was. She had spent two weeks trying to memorize the sequence as noise, and in ninety seconds Daven's jacket had given it an order her brain could hold. "It's not forty facts," she said. "It's one thing happening."

"That's what Annika keeps telling me about math," Daven said. "She's very ebullient about it. It's exhausting." He crouched to check the snake, which had lifted its head, tongue flickering, clearly annoyed at being warm and captive in equal measure.

When Ms. Costa came out at noon, scrubbed and eating a yogurt, she listened to Jordyn explain the whole pathway, using Daven's jacket as a visual aid while he held his arms out like a scarecrow. Ms. Costa didn't correct anything. She only asked one question, about what the ribosome was actually reading, and Jordyn got it right, mostly, and admitted the part she was still shaky on instead of pretending. Ms. Costa said that was the difference between someone who would learn the material and someone who would use it, and told them both to wash their hands before they touched anything else in her clinic.

Outside, in the parking lot, Daven straddled his bike. "So he's going to be okay?"

"He'll be okay by Monday if he keeps eating. Ms. Costa said release him near the pond where the sun hits." Jordyn folded her flashcards, all forty of them, now just one idea wearing forty costumes, and slid the rubber band off the deck. "Hey. The quiz you gave me helped more than three days of studying. Do it again sometime?"

Daven, who had spent all of junior year insisting he was strictly a physics person, went a little pink. "I guess I remember more than I thought," he said, and zipped his jacket halfway back up, then stopped. "Half a helix for the road," and rode off grinning with the zipper still open.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: Braking distance is proportional to the square of speed, so doubling a car's speed makes the distance needed to brake about four times as long.
story:
The car was Mr. Santoso's, a silver hatchback that smelled of mints and old paper, and he had cleared the passenger seat of its usual folders so Mya could imagine, as he put it, that the car belonged to her. The street outside his house was empty in the way suburban streets are empty at eight on a Saturday, when everyone's cars sit in driveways and the sprinklers do their slow work. Mya adjusted the mirror, though she did not need to, because adjusting it was something she could do correctly.

"Seat, mirrors, seatbelt," Mr. Santoso said. "In that order, every time, until it's not an order anymore. Until it's just how you sit down." He had a way of speaking that made instructions sound like observations about the weather. She had known him for years as the neighbour who reseeded his lawn in September, and it was strange to find him suddenly an authority, although her mother said he had taught half the kids on this street.

Mya's mother had a theory of driving, which was that it was the most dangerous thing a normal person ever does on purpose. Her mother quoted statistics at dinner. Cecilia, meanwhile, had a theory of her own, acquired over the summer between prom and August, which was that the whole point of being young was to feel the speed of things, windows down, music up, what she called, with total sincerity, a little bit of hedonism. Mya had listened to both of them that morning over cereal, saying nothing, and had come to Mr. Santoso's driveway carrying the two opinions like bags she could not set down.

She pulled out of the driveway on the second attempt, the first having ended in a stall that Mr. Santoso absorbed without comment. They drove to the end of the street, turned at the cul-de-sac where the Niemans' hydrangeas leaned over the curb, and came back. At fifteen miles an hour the street was almost too slow to be interesting. A crow walked across the road in front of them and had time to reconsider.

"Here's a question," Mr. Santoso said, as she brought the car to a smooth stop at the stop sign at the corner of Alder. "You stopped from fifteen just now. Suppose you were going thirty. Twice the speed. How much longer does the car need to stop?"

"Twice as long," Mya said. It seemed obvious. Distance was speed times time; she had parametrized the problem that way without noticing, the way she did in physics class, and twice the speed gave twice the distance. "Thirty is double fifteen, so double the stopping distance."

"That's what nearly everybody says." He rolled down his window an inch, letting in the smell of cut grass. "Try it and see."

They found the long straight stretch of Alder where the houses sat farther apart and no one was walking a dog. He had her accelerate to fifteen, brake hard at the cracked mailbox he'd chosen, and she stopped well short of it, the belt tightening across her chest, a small visceral shock, the first time the car had pushed back against her. Then he had her do it again at thirty. She started braking at the same mailbox, certain she would stop in twice the room, and the car kept going, past the mailbox, past the driveway after it, the tires gripping and complaining, until the hatchback finally settled almost four houses' worth of lawn away from where she'd first touched the pedal.

They sat for a moment with the engine ticking. Mya looked back at the mailbox, small in the mirror now, and did the arithmetic in reverse. Twice the speed, and the distance had not doubled, it had come out to about four times as long. She said it out loud to make it real. "So doubling speed doesn't double braking distance. The distance goes up with the square of the speed. It's squared."

"That's the one," Mr. Santoso said. "Braking distance grows with the square of your speed. Double how fast you're going and you need roughly four times the room to stop." He said it lightly, the way he'd said seat, mirrors, seatbelt, as if it were a fact of weather. "People's instincts are linear. The road isn't."

Mya thought of Cecilia taking the curve onto the parkway at sixty with three people in the back, and of her mother quoting statistics, and found that neither of them had ever said this, that the danger did not grow evenly with speed but leapt ahead of it, quietly, mathematically, a curve bending away from intuition. Her mother's fear was still too blunt, Cecilia's thrill still too easy, but they were arguing over the same curve from opposite ends. She did not know yet where on it she would choose to sit. That, she suspected, would take longer than one lesson to find out.

They drove back toward his house at a careful twenty, past the sprinklers, past the Nieman hydrangeas, and when the crow appeared again in the road ahead, unhurried as before, Mya eased off the gas early and let the car slow by itself.

"There's the second one," Mr. Santoso said, watching the bird clear the curb. "Take us home."

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Fat bloom is a dull grey or white streaky film that appears on chocolate that was not properly tempered or has melted and reset.
story:
Logan stood at Kenny's kitchen counter with a bowl of melted chocolate in front of him and a thermometer clipped to the side of it. The plan had started two weeks ago, when he found the box of chocolates he'd left in his car through a July afternoon. The pieces had reset with dull grey streaks across their tops, white and mottled like frost on a window, and when he snapped one it bent instead of breaking. He'd brought the box to school and set it on the lunch table between Kenny and Alaina.

"That's called fat bloom," Alaina said, turning a piece over in the light. "My mom gets it on the chocolate she leaves in the car. It's still fine to eat, it just looks terrible."

"Fat bloom," Logan repeated, and that was the beginning of it. He wanted to make chocolates for his mother's birthday, real ones, glossy and hard, the kind that snapped when you bit them, and he'd learned by now that the difference between that and the streaky grey stuff was something called tempering.

Kenny's kitchen was the venue because Kenny's mother worked Saturdays and Kenny had a double boiler, or the remains of one: a metal bowl balanced over a saucepan whose handle had gone obsolescent years ago and finally snapped off in the spring. They used a wooden spoon to stir.

The method Logan had printed out from the library computer called for three stages. Melt the chocolate to about forty-five degrees. Cool it to twenty-seven, working a portion of it on a marble slab or, in their case, a baking sheet, with a spatula, folding it over itself. Then rewarm it gently to thirty-one and a half, and hold it there. If it went higher, they'd have to start over. He'd read the numbers so many times he could say them in his sleep, but the paper itself had gone soft with steam and the print had begun to run, so that the final stage was now only adumbrated by a grey smear where the temperature had been.

"You have to be able to read that," Kenny said, peering at the page.

"I know it. Thirty-one and a half."

They poured the melted chocolate onto the sheet and spread it with the spatula, pushing it back and forth, and Logan watched it thicken from loose and brown to something with a matte body, dragging at the edge of the blade. His arms ached. Kenny timed him on his phone, calling out every thirty seconds, and Logan kept folding, sweat at his hairline, until the chocolate held a ridge when the spatula lifted.

Back into the bowl, over the warm water, a few degrees at a time. Alaina arrived halfway through with the ruined box from the car, which she'd kept, for reasons she didn't explain, in the pocket of her jacket. She lined four of the grey-streaked pieces along the counter like evidence. "For comparison," she said.

At thirty-one and a half they dipped. Logan had brought strawberries and a bar of hazelnuts chopped fine, and he pushed each berry through the chocolate with two fingers, laid it on waxed paper, and waited. The waiting was the hard part. Kenny wanted to touch them. Kenny touched one, and left a thumbprint shaped like a crescent, and Logan made him wash his hands and sit on a stool across the room.

The chocolate set in the kitchen's cool, in about five minutes, without a fridge. When Logan picked up a strawberry, the shell had a hard shine to it, and he broke off the leaf end with a clean sound, a snap like a small branch. He held the broken edge beside Alaina's grey pieces, side by side on the counter. The streaked chocolate looked older, tired, as though it had been through something the new batch had not.

"So that's the difference," Alaina said. "That's what happens when you do it right."

"Or when it doesn't melt and reset on the way to the house," Logan said. He was thinking of the drive over, the bowl wrapped in towels on the passenger seat, the sun through the windshield. He turned the berry in his fingers. "I don't actually know if I can do this twice. It could've been luck."

"Then do it twice," Kenny said, already reaching for the second bar.

Logan weighed out the new chocolate, still holding the first snapped piece, and put the bowl back over the water. From the hallway came the sound of a key in the lock, and then Mr. Luo, the neighbour who let himself in on Saturdays to borrow the paper, stood in the kitchen doorway.

"You made chocolates," Mr. Luo said. He was a gourmand of long standing, at least where his own kitchen was concerned, and he took one of Alaina's grey pieces without asking and ate it in two bites. He reached for a strawberry next.

"Take the streaky ones," Logan said, and moved the bowl of tempered chocolate out of his reach. "Those are the ones that melted in the car."

Mr. Luo picked up a grey piece anyway, turned it toward the window, and shrugged. Logan stirred the new batch and watched the thermometer climb.

activity: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
knowledge_domain: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
fact: Recipients in an email's Bcc field are hidden from everyone else, which is why messages to a long list of people who don't know each other often use Bcc to protect their addresses.
story:
The email was already drafted when Sara arrived at the community center on Tuesday morning, and Ms. Kovalenko was hovering over the send button like a woman about to jump. "Fifty parents," she said, tapping the screen. "Fifty families who signed up for the summer reading program, and every one of them wants the schedule. I put them all in one message so nobody misses it." Sara leaned in and saw the To field stacked with addresses, row after row of them, strangers to each other, all about to be handed over to everyone else.

Her stomach tightened, though she could not at first say why. She was sixteen and this was her second week of an internship she had begged for, filing forms and refilling the coffee maker, and the last thing she wanted was to correct a woman who had been generous with her time, almost munificent, letting Sara sit in on staff meetings and take real notes. But she had learned something in her computer applications class that kept pushing at her. "Ms. Kovalenko," she said, and her voice came out smaller than she intended, "do you know about Bcc?"

Ms. Kovalenko turned, one eyebrow raised. "The blind copy field," Eshan said from the supply closet doorway, where he had been counting markers for the craft bins. He was the other intern, a boy from Sara's school who argued about everything but whose opinions she had started, reluctantly, to trust. "Recipients in the Bcc field are hidden from everyone else." Sara nodded, relieved not to be alone in it. "That's why messages to a long list of people who don't know each other often use it," she said. "It protects their addresses. If you send it like this, every parent gets every other parent's email, and some of them might not want that."

Ms. Kovalenko frowned at the screen. "These are parents of children in the same program. They will meet each other at the kickoff picnic. What is there to hide?" Sara felt the question land like a test, and she understood that the answer had to be more careful than her first instinct, which was to say it was just obviously rude. "It's not about hiding," she said slowly, working it out as she spoke. "It's about deciding for them. Some of these families are dealing with, you know, custody things. One of the intake forms mentioned a subpoena over a custody dispute, actually, a word I had to look up last week. If a father's new address goes out to fifty strangers, that's his information, not ours to share."

The room went quiet except for the hum of the ancient printer. Eshan crossed his arms. "Or you could just email them one at a time," he said. "Fifty separate messages. Completely private." Sara pictured it: Ms. Kovalenko, who stayed late every Thursday already, sending fifty individual emails by hand. "That protects them better," she admitted, "but it takes an hour she doesn't have, and if one gets mistyped someone gets nothing at all." She looked at the To field again. The two ideas sat side by side in her head, privacy and practicality, and neither one was wrong. "Bcc is the middle," she said. "One message, everyone gets it, nobody sees the list."

Ms. Kovalenko did not answer right away, and Sara braced herself for dismissal. Instead the older woman pulled out a chair and sat down heavily. "You know," she said, "I ran this program for eleven years on paper. Sign-up sheets on a clipboard. I never had to think about who could see whom." She read the draft again, her lips moving. Then she clicked into the To field, selected all fifty addresses, cut them, and pasted them into the line below. The To field now held only the program's own office address. "Like that?" she asked.

"Like that," Sara said, and then, because she wanted to be honest rather than triumphant, "I think. I'm not certain whether the office address in To looks strange to parents. Maybe a line explaining it would help. Something like, 'You are receiving this as part of the reading program list.'" Ms. Kovalenko tilted her head, considering. "A line of explanation. Professional and clear." She typed it, read it aloud, and changed "you are receiving" to "you are receiving this schedule," which somehow made it sound less like a legal notice and more like a person talking.

When the send finally happened, Sara watched the progress bar crawl and felt something loosen in her chest. Eshan drifted over and nudged her shoulder with his. "You realize you just told your supervisor she was wrong on your second week," he said. "I told her she had options," Sara said. "There's a difference." She was still turning that difference over, uncertain where flattery ended and respect began, when Ms. Kovalenko spun her chair around. "Sara. Next week I have to ask the donors for money. Sixty of them. Do you want to draft that one?"

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
