fact: Form V cocoa butter crystals melt at about 33.8 degrees Celsius, just below body temperature, which is why well-tempered chocolate melts in the mouth but not in the hand.
story:
The kitchen of the restaurant had one window, and through it Alexis could see the tents going up in the parking lot for Saturday's farmers' market. He stood at the marble slab with a bench scraper in his hand, watching Mr. Rao pour a ribbon of dark chocolate onto the cold stone. "You want it moving," Mr. Rao said. "Always moving. Chocolate punishes standing still." Alexis was eighteen, two weeks out of high school, and this was his first job that wasn't mowing lawns. He'd taken it because he wanted to be a pastry chef, or thought he did, though lately that want had begun to feel more like a guess he'd made about himself at fifteen and never checked.

"Form V," Mr. Rao said, tapping the thermometer. "That's what we're after. The stable crystals." Then he walked away to deal with a delivery of strawberries, because Mr. Rao believed in explaining one sentence's worth and leaving the rest to your hands.

Alexis spread the chocolate with the scraper, gathered it, spread it again. The streaks on the marble went from glossy to matte as the temperature dropped. When Mr. Rao came back, he touched the edge of a test strip that had set on parchment, and it snapped under his thumb with a sound like a knuckle cracking. "That," he said, "is what you're listening for." Alexis wrote SNAP in his notebook, felt ridiculous, kept the notebook anyway.

He got it wrong twice that first week. One batch set dull and streaked, soft at the corners, and Mr. Rao had him scrape the whole thing back into the melter without comment, which was somehow worse than shouting. The second failure was stranger: the chocolate set shiny but bent instead of snapping, and Alexis sat on the loading dock afterward eating the ruined scraps, thinking about how he'd defended his college choice to Said in the parking lot of the school in June. "You're going to study philosophy and make croissants," Said had said, delighted with himself. "You're the most cerebral person I know who owns steel-toed boots." Alexis had laughed and not answered, because the honest answer was that he didn't know whether the philosophy part was him or just something he was good at, a costume he'd worn so long it had fused to the skin.

On Saturday he worked the market stall with Noa, who'd been at the restaurant a year longer and had a driver's license and no patience for anything she couldn't eat. They arranged bars and dipped strawberries under the white tent. The morning was already warm, and Alexis kept touching the display chocolate, expecting disaster. It stayed solid. A woman with a toddler bought a bar, set it on the table while she counted change, and it sat there holding its shape in the sun-flecked heat. Then her little boy grabbed a piece and it vanished into his mouth and he went quiet in a way that made three separate people laugh.

"Why does it do that," Noa said, gesturing at the table and then at the kid. "It's warm out. Why isn't it a puddle?"

Alexis opened his mouth and then closed it, because he realized he knew, and knowing it felt like the first time all summer something had actually stuck. "Form V cocoa butter crystals melt at about 33.8 degrees Celsius," he said. "Just below body temperature. That's why well-tempered chocolate melts in the mouth but not in the hand." He heard how it sounded, like a recitation, and Noa raised an eyebrows at him.

"That's the most romantic thing anyone's ever said to me," she said, and stole a strawberry.

But he'd been thinking about it since Tuesday, in fact, when his philosophy class habit had resurfaced and he'd caught himself trying to historicize the whole business: chocolate as a colonial commodity, temperature as a historically contingent standard, the clean snap of a well-made bar as an aesthetic the pastry world had only recently agreed to prize. That had seemed like real thinking at one in the morning. At nine, at the marble slab, it had seemed like a way of not learning to use a scraper. The two halves of him, the one that wanted to historicize and the one that wanted to temper, had been standing on opposite sides of the kitchen all summer, and neither would admit the other was also him.

The toddler's mother came back for a second bar. "He never sits still for food," she said, almost apologetic, and Noa said, "That's the ontology of good chocolate, it stops children," and Alexis laughed so hard he had to lean on the table. "That's not what ontology means," he said. "But keep going. That was better than most of my seminars."

What he hadn't worked out, and told no one, was whether he would go back to the philosophy department in the fall or defer a semester, or a year, or forever. His father wanted an answer by the end of August. Alexis had changed his mind three times in July alone, and the last change had come at the slab: he'd been spreading chocolate, thinking about Form V, about how the stable form was the one you got only by cooling slowly and agitating constantly, never by rushing or by standing still, and he'd thought, without wanting to, that a person might work the same way. He distrusted the thought immediately. It was exactly the kind of tidy metaphor a philosophy student would build a paper on, and it proved nothing about semesters. And yet it kept coming back every time the chocolate snapped clean.

Sunday night, closing the kitchen, he found Mr. Rao doing inventory by the walk-in light. "Ask your question," Mr. Rao said, without looking up. Alexis asked whether the melting point meant you could temper by feel, without the thermometer, just by the heat of your fingers. Mr. Rao finally looked at him. "Try it," he said. "Report back." So Alexis got a bowl, melted a bar, and held his fingertip to the surface, waiting, agitating, watching the gloss shift, trusting his own body temperature to tell him when he was a fraction of a degree from the truth.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: In plant and animal cells, introns are cut out of newly made RNA and the remaining exons are spliced together before the messenger RNA leaves the nucleus.
story:
Ryder had failed the first biology test of the semester, and the deal his father offered that night was simple: pass the retake on Friday, or the money set aside for his camera lens would be redirected, with insulting tidiness, into what his father called an annuity for his future self, a phrase Ryder found almost deliberately joyless. He cared about the lens. He cared about the test only as a doorway to the lens, which he understood was not a noble reason to learn anything, and which he decided not to examine too closely.

The problem was the second half of the unit, the part about how DNA actually got used. He could parrot the words, transcription and translation, the way you can recite lyrics to a song in a language you don't speak. On Wednesday after school he sat in the library with Susan, who had gotten a 96 and who explained things by gesticulating with both hands until the librarian twice looked over.

"So the DNA is copied into RNA," Susan said, drawing a squiggle. "That's transcription. Then the RNA gets read out and a protein gets built. That's translation."

"Copied into RNA, then protein. Fine. Why is there a middle step at all?"

Susan opened her mouth, closed it, and said, "Mr. Campbell would say that's a good question."

Ryder took that as meaning she didn't know either, which was strangely comforting.

That night, instead of studying, he did what he always did instead of studying: he opened his editing software. He and Rian had filmed a skit over the weekend, twelve minutes of raw footage for what would be a three-minute video, and Ryder's job was to cut it. He dragged the bad takes onto the timeline, watched Rian flub a line, delete that clip, watch himself laugh at Rian flubbing the line, keep that clip because the laughter was funnier than the joke, delete the actual joke. Slowly the twelve minutes compressed into something that moved. He did not send it out piecemeal, the good bits with the bad bits still stuck between them. He assembled the whole thing first, in his laptop, and only when it was finished and coherent did he export it and send it to Rian.

He was reaching for his textbook to force himself back to biology when the thought arrived, fully formed and slightly unfair, that he already knew this. The raw footage was the newly made RNA, long and full of nonsense. The clips he cut out were the junk parts, the introns. The parts he kept, the exons, got spliced together into a message that actually made sense. And just like his video, which only left his laptop once it was finished, the messenger RNA only left the nucleus after the cutting and splicing was done. In plant and animal cells, the introns get cut out of the new RNA, the remaining exons get spliced together, and only then does the messenger RNA leave the nucleus.

He sat very still for a moment, then texted Rian: "wait. I just figured out bio from editing our video. the bad takes I cut out are like introns. the good clips are exons and I splice them together before it leaves my laptop, like mRNA leaving the nucleus. I'm a cell."

Rian replied four minutes later with a single line: "so when I ruined nine takes of the same joke I was intron material?"

"Yes," Ryder typed. "You were noncoding regions of Rian."

Rian sent back a thumbs up and the message "splice me out of the credits then," which Ryder interpreted, generously, as a joke and less generously as a small true wound.

On Thursday Ryder tested his understanding against Susan at lunch, and it mostly held. But there was one thing that snagged. "Okay," Susan said, chewing, "but here's what I don't get. Sometimes the cell cuts the RNA differently and keeps parts it cut before. Same DNA, different protein." She showed him a diagram in the textbook, alternative splicing, and Ryder felt his neat video metaphor wobble. His edit had been his choice, his taste. Who was choosing inside the cell, and how did it decide?

That was the question he took to Mr. Campbell before class on Friday, the retake folded into his backpack. "I think I understand it," Ryder said, "but I don't understand who's doing the editing, or how it knows what to keep."

Mr. Campbell, who was watering an auxiliary tray of seedlings by the window, set down the watering can. "That's a real question," he said. "People are still working on it. You can know the steps and not know that."

"Can I pass the test anyway?"

"You can pass the test and still not know that," Mr. Campbell said, and turned back to the seedlings.

In the gym during the retake, Ryder wrote out the whole sequence, DNA copied into RNA, introns cut out, exons spliced together, the finished messenger RNA leaving the nucleus, and he drew a small laptop next to the nucleus with an arrow, which he then erased in case it looked like cheating. He left the question of who was doing the editing at the bottom of the page, unanswered, not because he ran out of time but because he didn't want to pretend. Outside the window Rian was walking across the parking lot, and Ryder, filling in the last scantron bubble, thought about the video still unsent, still sitting finished in his laptop, and how he'd splice it tomorrow, or maybe leave it in a little longer.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: Larger samples give more precise estimates, so a result from a small study carries a wider margin of error than the same result from a large one.
story:
Layla spread the two articles across the cafe table like cards she intended to read, though she had read each three times already and understood neither one any better for it. The first, from a psychology journal, reported that students who handwrote their notes remembered more than students who typed. The second, from an education journal, reported the same thing. Same question, same answer, and for two days she had been sitting with the strange problem that agreement had given her nothing to say.

Deshawn came in with his backpack over one shoulder, ordered an iced americano even though it was November, and dropped into the chair opposite her. "You look like the review's winning," he said.

"It's not a review yet. It's two summaries stapled together in my head." She turned the pages so he could see. "This one had thirty students, a single lecture, one recall test a week later. This one had thirty thousand. And they both found the same effect, so Ms. Zhu's rubric wants me to compare them, and I keep writing 'both studies agree,' which is a sentence that takes four words and gets me nothing."

Deshawn leaned over and squinted at a table of numbers. "So if they agree, what's the paper about?"

"That's the thing I can't figure out." She pulled her laptop closer and opened the draft, scrolling past her introduction, which she had rewritten five times, to the paragraph where she had written that the smaller study "lends additional support" to the larger one. She had liked that phrase when she wrote it. Now it sat on the screen looking thinner every time she looked. "I think I've had it backwards this whole time."

Ms. Zhu came in at four, the way she did most Thursdays, and stood at the counter waiting for a cappuccino. Layla watched her and did not wave. The assignment sheet had said, in its last line, that the review should adjudicate between sources, and Layla had looked up the word and then set it aside, because she could not see what there was to adjudicate between two studies that said the same thing.

She looked at the numbers again. The small study's result sat inside a wide band, generous enough that the true effect could have been almost anything in a broad range. The large study's same result sat inside a band so narrow it looked like a pen stroke. She read the caption under the table, then read it again. "Okay," she said slowly. "Here's something. The small one is the weak one. Even though it found the same thing. Thirty people, and the estimate has a much wider margin of error. Thirty thousand, and the margin's tiny. So the small study doesn't support the big one. The big one just doesn't need the support."

"So your paper says the big study wins?"

"It's not a fight. That's what I was getting wrong." She was already deleting the sentence about additional support. "They agree, but one of them knows what it found and the other one found something it can only point at. If I trust the small one alone, I'm trusting a number that could really be anywhere in that band. The same number from the big study means something different, because the margin of error is narrower. The finding is the same. The finding isn't the same. Both of those are true and I have to hold them at the same time, which is apparently what a review is."

Deshawn turned his cup in its ring of condensation. "So which one do you believe?"

"That's not the right question either." She heard how pretentious it sounded and said it anyway, because it was accurate. "I believe the large one more, and I can't fully say why beyond the margin, and there's a paragraph where I have to be honest about what I still can't tell from either of them. Like whether the effect happens in real classes or only in labs. Neither study touches that. Thirty thousand people is a lot of people, but they were all still doing the same artificial task." She stopped, because she was talking faster than she was writing, and pulled the laptop back.

She typed for a while. The cafe filled with the after-work crowd, and the espresso machine went from occasional to constant, a hiss and a clatter every ninety seconds. At the table by the window, a man argued on his phone in a low, sullen monotone, and the barista asked him twice to take it outside before he did. Deshawn worked on something of his own, or pretended to; mostly he watched Layla's face while she read and deleted and read again.

When Ms. Zhu left, she stopped at their table on her way to the door. "How's the review coming?"

"Better. I was treating the two articles like they were the same because they got the same answer, and they're not, because the small one has this huge margin of error and the big one barely has any. Larger samples, narrower margins. That's the whole spine of my argument now."

Ms. Zhu nodded once, said "Good, that's a real observation," and was gone before Layla could ask whether it was the observation she'd been supposed to find or one she'd found by happenstance, wandering in through the side door of a caption she'd almost skipped.

At six, Deshawn packed up and left, and Layla stayed to finish the paragraph about what remained uncertain. She saved the file, closed the laptop, and began stacking the articles, the small one on top. As she slid them into her folder she noticed, for the first time, the funding disclosure on its final page: the large study, the one with thirty thousand participants and the margin like a hairline, had been paid for by a company that sells smartpens, the kind that record what you write. The small, sloppy, thirty-person study had been run on a departmental budget by two graduate students with no disclosure at all.

She stood at the cafe door with the folder under her arm, not moving, while the cold came in around her ankles. Then she went back to the table, opened the laptop, and started a new paragraph.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: Most US and Canadian jurisdictions use graduated licensing, in which new drivers move from a learner's permit to a provisional license with restrictions before a full license.
story:
The parking lot behind the shuttered grocery store had been empty so long that weeds had desiccated in the seams of the asphalt, their pale stalks bowing in every crack. Joseph sat behind the wheel of Mr. Vu's Corolla with his hands at ten and two, the way the pamphlet had shown, while Mr. Vu stood outside the driver's door drinking coffee from a thermos lid, watching him the way a man watches weather he does not trust.

"Foot on the brake, then start it," Mr. Vu said. He was a neighbor, retired, dour in the mornings and almost cheerful by dinner, and he had agreed to this only after Joseph's mother had asked him three times. Joseph turned the key. The engine caught, and the whole car seemed to gather itself under him like a sleeping animal aware of being watched.

He let the brake up an inch. They rolled. He steered a slow, wobbling oval around the cart corrals, and on the second lap he even touched the gas, and the lot widened around him, and for one clean half minute he understood why people loved this. He had promised Jaycee he would drive her to her community college audition next month, the one with the tuba in the back seat, the one she had been rehearsing for since October. He had promised her in the school hallway with Keith standing there as witness, which in their grade was nearly a notarized document.

Keith arrived on his bike around the third lap, coasting to a stop against the light pole. "You got the permit?" he called. Joseph braked more sharply than he meant to and the seat belt bit his collarbone. "Yesterday," he said through the window. "Why do you think I'm doing circles in the Dead Mart lot at nine in the morning." Keith pulled a folded paper from his jacket, the printout Joseph had left on Keith's kitchen table, and read from it with mock ceremony. "It says here, 'Most US and Canadian jurisdictions use graduated licensing.'" He looked up. "Graduated. Like you're moving up a ladder, not getting a key to everything."

Joseph put the car in park and held out his hand for the paper. The paragraphs were short and dry, and the second one flattened his morning. A permit, then a provisional license with restrictions, and only after that a full license. He read the line twice. "So I can't just take the test next week and drive whoever I want," he said.

"Whoever," Keith said, grinning. "Like, hypothetically, a tuba player." He was enjoying this more than the morning warranted, but Keith had wanted the solo spot in jazz band that Jaycee had won, and though he never said anything sour about it, he did not mind watching Joseph's promises run aground either. Joseph read further, muttering the order of it to himself, permit to provisional to full, as if saying it aloud would negotiate it down.

He thought of his cousin, two years older, who had talked about driving the way a pundit on television talks about the economy, all confidence and no information, and who had still, after all that talk, spent a summer riding the bus because he had assumed one test was enough. Joseph had believed the same thing. He had built a favor on it. He looked up at Mr. Vu, who had come around to the hood and was finishing his coffee with the unhurried patience of a man who had watched many young people discover paperwork. "Did you know it works like this?" Joseph asked him. Mr. Vu shrugged. "Where I grew up, it was one test and good luck." He drained the lid and screwed it back onto the thermos. "Circle the other way now. You're favoring your left."

Joseph circled the other way, and the steering felt stranger, and he clipped a curb on the fourth turn, a small hard jolt that rang up through his wrists. He stopped, breathed, started again. He thought of last October, the audition notice pinned to the band room door, the way Jaycee had gone quiet and then said she would go but that the bus took two hours and the route missed the warm-up time entirely. She had a workaround, she'd said, her father could take her if his shift changed, but the shift had not changed in three years. She had said all of this without asking him for anything, which was exactly why he had promised. There had been a moment in the hallway, Keith a few lockers down, when offering the ride had felt less like generosity and more like announcing who he was going to be.

He parked between two faded lines and got out. The morning had warmed, and the weeds around the lot's edges had stopped being dead-looking and started looking merely dormant, waiting out the season. "The audition is in five weeks," he said to Keith. "Say the earliest I pass the road test, I'm still on the provisional thing. It has restrictions. I don't even know yet what all of them are." He folded the printout and put it in his back pocket. "But her father's shift is Saturday nights, and the audition's a Saturday morning. That part might actually line up."

Keith straddled his bike, unconvinced but listening. Mr. Vu locked the Corolla and lifted the thermos in something like a salute. "Same time Thursday," he said. "Practice the parking until you hate it, then practice it more." Joseph pulled out his phone to text Jaycee, typed and deleted two versions of the truth, and finally wrote only, "Driving lesson went good. Can I call you tonight?" Across the lot, a sparrow landed on the cart corral and began, with what seemed like pure stubbornness, to pull a dry stalk out of the crack in the asphalt.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: In October 2024 the Los Angeles Times did not endorse a presidential candidate after its owner blocked the editorial board's plans, and several board members resigned in protest.
story:
The print deadline was six o'clock, and at four Lily still had a blank half page where the editorial belonged. She spread the drafts across the library table under the long windows, and the paper looked thin, almost diaphanous in the late light, as if the argument hadn't enough substance to hold ink.

"The principal wants to read it first," Molly said, dropping into the chair across from her. "Before we print. That's what he told Audrina."

"He told her it was a courtesy."

"He told her he'd pull the printing budget if it wasn't."

The editorial argued that the district was planning to cut the theatre program while adding a second turf field, and that the numbers the superintendent had released didn't add up. Lily had the documents. She had the coach's own admission, on tape, that the field contract had gone to a firm where a school board member's brother worked. What she didn't have was a way to print any of it under a principal who read first and cut second.

She went to the front desk, where Ms. Papadopoulos was checking in a cart of returns. "I need stuff on newspaper ownership," Lily said. "Like, who decides what a paper can say."

"Media section, aisle four. Start with the recent histories." Ms. Papadopoulos stamped a date due and didn't look up, which Lily appreciated. She didn't want a conversation. She wanted ammunition.

Aisle four smelled of old glue and radiator dust. Lily found the book Ms. Papadopoulos had shelved face-out, something about the last decade of American newspapers, and sat down on the carpet between the stacks with it open on her knees. She read fast, skimming, until a paragraph stopped her. In October 2024 the Los Angeles Times had planned to endorse a presidential candidate. Its owner blocked the plan. The paper endorsed no one, and several members of the editorial board resigned in protest. Lily read the paragraph twice, then took out her phone and confirmed it in a second source, because Ms. Papadopoulos had drilled that into every student who ever cited anything in this building.

"Find anything?" Audrina had come down the aisle, arms crossed, coat still on.

"October 2024," Lily said. "The LA Times. The owner blocked the endorsement the editorial board wanted to make, so the paper endorsed nobody, and several board members resigned."

Audrina stood very still. "Resigned. Like, quit the whole paper."

"Over the endorsement."

Audrina sat down on the carpet too, slowly, the way you sit when something has shifted under you. She had been the one who told the principal, politely, that the paper was a student paper. Now she was quiet for the length of a radiator tick.

Lily tried to metabolize what she was feeling, which was not exactly courage and not exactly fear, more a rearrangement. She had spent the week thinking the problem was whether her facts were solid. The facts were solid. The problem was that the facts were going to travel through a machine owned by someone with an interest in them not arriving. That wasn't relativism, some position where every version of events was equally true. The turf contract either went to the board member's brother or it didn't. It did. The question was only who paid for the paper it got printed on.

"If we print without showing him, he kills the budget next semester," Audrina said. "If we show him, he kills this issue."

"Or he reads it and lets it go."

"He won't."

"I know."

Outside the window the parking lot lights came on, one bank at a time, and Lily watched them flicker to full brightness against a sky going violet. She looked at the open book on her knees, at the board members who had walked out of one of the biggest newspapers in the country rather than stay silent inside it, and she understood that their resignations were not the same thing as publication. The story still got told, but elsewhere, by others, in fragments. And she understood something else, which was that she and Molly and Audrina had no elsewhere. This paper, printed on the school's risograph with the school's ink, was the only press they had.

"Here's what stays true no matter what he does," Lily said, closing the book. "The field contract, the brother, the cut theatre budget. That doesn't change if we print or don't. What changes is whether we're the ones who said it."

"So we print."

"We print, and we hand him a copy at seven a.m., after it's already off the press. And if he cuts the budget, we publish it as a PDF and tape it to the gym doors."

Audrina laughed once, short, not really a laugh. "He'll call our parents."

"He'll call our parents."

Molly appeared at the end of the aisle holding two coffees from the machine in the foyer, contraband under the no-food sign, steam rising thin from the lids. "Six o'clock still the deadline?" she said. "Because you two are sitting on the floor in aisle four and the layout's still got a hole in it."

Lily stood, brushed the carpet dust off her jeans, and carried the book back toward the table where the blank half page was waiting. She set the coffee down beside the drafts and began to type.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: The Common European Framework of Reference describes a B2 speaker as able to explain a viewpoint on a topical issue, giving the advantages and disadvantages of various options.
story:
Carson had been sitting on Natalya's kitchen floor for forty minutes with a stack of index cards fanned around him like a lost hand of solitaire. Her mother kept passing through to refill a glass of water she wasn't drinking, which was her way of eavesdropping without appearing to, and every time she passed, Carson shuffled the cards into a different order, as though fluency were a matter of sorting.

"Again," said Natalya, from the counter, where she was slicing an apple with surgical indifference. "Five minutes. Spanish. No English, no dying dramatically on the floor."

"I wasn't dying dramatically. I was pausing to think."

"You said 'el, el, el' for eleven seconds. I counted."

The assignment sheet lay beside the fruit bowl, and Carson had read it so many times the folds had gone soft. Five minutes, topical issue, Spanish III Honors, and at the bottom, in Ms. Ramírez's tidy hand, a note: students should be performing at B2. He'd looked it up last night and written the definition on a card, which he now held up like a lawyer presenting evidence. "The Common European Framework describes a B2 speaker as able to explain a viewpoint on a topical issue, giving the advantages and disadvantages of various options."

"Read that to yourself, not to me," Natalya said. "I'm the timer, not the jury."

Christophe arrived then, ebullient, still carrying his gym bag, having come straight from a debate team practice he described as "the trial of the century" because the topic had been whether prosecutors should be able to appeal an acquittal. He dropped onto a chair, stole a slice of apple, and said, "So what's your issue, Carson? Make it juicy."

"Congestion pricing," Carson said. "Whether the city should charge drivers to enter downtown."

Christophe groaned with pleasure. "Tolls. Revenue. Fairness. You could amortize the whole transportation budget over twenty years and argue about it forever."

"I don't know what that means and I'm not saying it in Spanish," Carson said, and Natalya laughed so hard she had to set down the knife.

The first run collapsed inside ninety seconds. He had the arguments, he genuinely did; that was the infuriating part. He knew the tolls would fund the buses, he knew the fees fell hardest on people who drove because the trains didn't reach them, he had a card that said precisely this in his own cramped handwriting. But between his brain and his mouth stood a border checkpoint, and the guard kept asking for papers. He said "las ventajas" four times in one sentence. He called a bus "el autobús" and then, in a moment of pure panic, "la estación." He wanted to say the poor would pay a larger share of their income and instead announced, to the refrigerator, that the poor would pay a larger share of their house.

"Stop," Natalya said, not unkindly. "You're translating. Every sentence, English first, then customs."

"So what do I do instead?"

"Think in it badly. Badly is fine. B2 people are not poets."

He looked at his card again, the one with the definition, and something about it rearranged itself in his head. The sentence he'd been building, the long one with the subordinate clause and the subjunctive he wasn't sure he'd earned, wasn't actually necessary. The framework didn't want his best English thought wearing a costume. It wanted a viewpoint, advantages, disadvantages. Short roads, well lit. He turned the card over and wrote, in English because that part was still allowed: forget the essay. Just say where you stand, then both sides, like telling Christophe about a movie.

The second run went differently, not because his Spanish improved, but because he stopped building sentences from the foundations up. He stood where he stood. The tolls were fair in principle and cruel in the details, and that was true in any language, and he simply said it, in short crooked sentences that Natalya could have corrected and mercifully didn't. When he stumbled, he said "espera," and started the road again from a place he could see. The clock on the stove said four minutes fifty when he ran out of things to say and sat down on the floor among his cards.

"So which side wins?" Christophe asked, mouth full of apple.

"Neither," Carson said. "The tolls pay for the buses, so the person who can't afford the toll is funding the bus they might not be able to take. That part I can't fix with a position. I can only say it."

"In Spanish?"

"In Spanish."

Natalya reset the stove timer and held up the apple knife like a starting pistol. "Once more, from the top. And this time, don't look at the refrigerator like it owes you money."

"Espera," Carson said, and stood up.

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: In common-law jurisdictions, including most of the US, a contract made by a minor is generally voidable by the minor, with exceptions such as contracts for necessities.
story:
The rental counter sat between a shuttered coffee kiosk and a bank of phones nobody used anymore, and behind it a clerk in a gray vest was already sliding a clipboard toward Anna before she had fully set down her duffel. She was eighteen as of March, which she had repeated to her mother twice on the drive to the airport and once to Haylie in the parking garage, less as information than as a door she could finally walk through. Haylie stood beside her with her own bag, seventeen until October, bouncing slightly on her heels.

"Full-size or intermediate?" the clerk asked, tapping the screen without looking up.

"Intermediate," Anna said, because her mother had told her to, and then, quieter, "Two drivers."

The clerk's eyes came up at that. He asked for both licenses, turned Haylie's over twice, and set it back on the counter without pushing it toward her again. "I can't add her as a driver. Underage." Haylie opened her mouth, and he held up one finger, patient, bored. "It's not company policy, it's the law. In common-law jurisdictions, including most of the US, a contract made by a minor is generally voidable by the minor. Exceptions for necessities, things like that. A rental car isn't a necessity." He said it the way a person says a phone number they've recited eleven thousand times.

"So I could sign," Haylie said, "and then just... undo it?"

"You could sign anything you want. That's the problem. Voidable by you, not by us. We're the ones holding the risk." He turned back to Anna as though Haylie had become briefly invisible. "You can sign as the sole driver. Additional liability coverage is twenty-two dollars a day."

Anna's first thought, which she was not proud of, was that the clerk had a scathing sort of efficiency, the kind that made you feel like an item moving along a belt. Her second thought was that Haylie had stopped bouncing. They had planned this trip for four months, a drive to the coast to see Haylie's father, who was out of some facility Anna's mother never named in full, and it had always been understood that they would split the driving, that Haylie would take the mountain sections where Anna's hands got stiff on the wheel.

"I'll sign," Anna said. "Just me."

The signature line was small and ordinary. She had expected signing something like this to feel like a threshold, a hinge, and instead her pen skipped once on the laminate and she had to retrace the second n. The clerk explained the terms while she initialed: fuel level, damage walk-around, late return fees. Every few sentences the word liability surfaced and sank again, like something swimming under the terms and conditions she scrolled past on the screen without reading, ticking the box that said she had.

"Whatever happens to the car, it's on me," Anna said in the garage, testing the sentence out loud.

"You make it sound noble," Haylie said. "It's a Corolla."

But on the second day, in the mountains, with the light going long and amber across the guardrails, Haylie asked to drive anyway. Not asked, exactly. She stood by the passenger door with her arms crossed, stoic in the way she got when she'd decided not to ask for things, and Anna almost missed it, almost got in on the left side out of habit.

"It's my dad," Haylie said finally. "I haven't seen him in two years and I'm going to arrive in the passenger seat of my own trip."

Anna thought about the counter, about the clerk's flat recitation. The rule existed, she understood now, not to protect kids from adults exactly, but to protect the other party, the one handing over the keys, the one whose risk a minor could dissolve with a phone call. If she let Haylie drive, she wasn't breaking the law; she was breaking the contract, and the contract was the only thing standing between her and everything the word liability contained. Her bank account had four hundred dollars in it. Her mother didn't know about the second driver idea, and wouldn't, and that was its own quiet weight.

"Ten miles," Anna said, and got out.

Haylie drove beautifully, actually, loose and easy, and for those ten miles Anna watched the road through the windshield the way you watch a borrowed thing, her breath held at each curve. On a switchback outside a town whose name she'd forget, a truck came wide and Haylie pulled right, and the right rear panel found a low stone post with a sound like a struck bell. Small. A dent the size of a paperback, paint scraped to gray metal.

They stood looking at it while the engine ticked. Haylie said she would pay for it, and Anna said okay, and both of them heard how thin the word was, how it rested on nothing, on Haylie's weekend shifts and whatever the damage appraisal would say. Anna found herself wanting to impugn the fairness of the whole arrangement, the counter, the age line, the clause she'd scrolled past, and found she couldn't honestly. She had signed. She had wanted to sign. The wanting and the owing had arrived in the same hand.

At a gas station outside the town, Haylie went in for sodas and came back with a small envelope from the machine, the kind of card you fill out and send, and on it she had already written a first line to her father. Anna held the envelope while Haylie backed them out of the lot, one hand on the wheel, eyes on the mirror, the scraped panel catching the last of the light.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Cocoa butter can crystallize in six different forms, and tempering aims to make most of it set in form V, the crystal form that gives shine and snap.
story:
Jordan's first batch had set overnight into something that looked like wet earth, and when he broke a corner off it bent, then crumbled, refusing to snap. He stood at the kitchen counter at seven in the morning with the pieces in his palm, because Krista's going-away party was tomorrow evening and he had promised her a bar of chocolate made by his own hands, the kind of promise that sounded casual at the time and now felt like a signed document.

The night before, he had melted the chocolate in a bowl over simmering water, poured it into a mold, and refrigerated it, which his mother had watched with the mild skepticism of someone who has baked for thirty years. "It'll be fine," she'd said, in the tone that could presage anything but fine. It was not fine. The surface was dull as old paint, and the texture was grainy, sugar and cocoa refusing to agree with each other, a little congress of dissident ingredients that would not unify under any refrigerator's rule.

So he sat on the floor of the living room with his phone and read, and the reading rearranged everything. Cocoa butter, it turned out, could crystallize in six different forms, and what he needed was for most of it to set in form V, the one crystal form that gave shine and snap. He read the sentence three times. Six forms. One of them the good one. The chocolate he had made had simply chosen wrong, or rather had been allowed to choose, left unsupervised in the dark of the fridge like a class without a teacher.

He texted Emerick, who was coming to the party and had, in Jordan's opinion, a bellicose way of arguing about anything technical. "Tempering," Emerick wrote back within a minute, which annoyed Jordan, because he had wanted to be the one who knew the word. "You have to temper it. My gran does it every Christmas." Jordan did not ask Emerick's gran for details. He had until tomorrow at six, and something in him wanted to do this himself, to understand it rather than follow a recipe like a set of orders.

Ms. MacLeod from next door was sweeping her porch when he went out to buy a thermometer, and she asked what the rush was for. When he told her, she stopped sweeping. "My husband used to do that," she said. "He'd sit with the bowl on his knees for an hour, just stirring." She did not offer to supervise, and he did not ask, but she said she'd leave her marble slab on the back step tonight if he wanted it, since marble held the cold and his counter was laminate. He carried the slab inside like something borrowed from a museum.

The second attempt began in the afternoon. He melted the chocolate hot, then poured two thirds of it onto the marble and worked it back and forth with a spatula, watching the gloss go matte and then come back, dragging and folding until the thermometer read what the article had said it should. Then he stirred the cooler mass back into the warm bowl. His mother drifted through the kitchen, saw the thermometer clipped to the pot, and quietly put the kettle somewhere else so its steam would not reach the counter. He noticed. He didn't say anything, but he noticed.

The trouble was that he could not see the crystals. He was arranging things too small to see, trusting a number on a glass tube to tell him whether six possible forms were voting, and whether form V had the majority. There was no way to check, the article admitted, except to pour and wait. He thought about his chemistry teacher saying that a theory you cannot watch work is still a theory, and about Emerick's gran, who apparently just knew by the way it felt under the spatula. He could see the appeal of both, the instruments and the hands, and he could not fully have either tonight.

He poured the tempered chocolate into the mold, tapped the air bubbles out against the counter, and left it on the marble slab in the cool pantry, not the fridge, because the fridge had betrayed him once already. Then he sat on the pantry floor with his phone timer running, doing nothing, which was its own discipline.

At nine he turned the mold over onto a sheet of parchment. The bar came out in one piece, and the top caught the overhead light and threw it back. He snapped a corner off. It broke clean, with a sound like a small dry branch, and the broken edge looked polished. He put the corner on his tongue and let it sit there, and then he texted Emerick a photo of the bar with no caption, and carried the whole thing across the dark yard to Ms. MacLeod's porch so she could see it before he wrapped it.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: Schenck v. United States introduced the 'clear and present danger' test, allowing speech to be punished if it created a clear and present danger of harm Congress could prevent.
story:
The polling station had been set up in the gymnasium of the old middle school, and Emily had chosen it deliberately, arriving two hours before her mock court presentation so she could watch democracy happen at its most ordinary while she tried to hold two opposing arguments in her head at once. Her civics class had drawn cases from a hat, and she had drawn Schenck v. United States, and Mr. Costa had informed her, with what she suspected was private amusement, that she would argue both sides before the panel of teachers assembled in the library that afternoon. Not one side and then a rebuttal of it. Both sides, in full, as though she were two lawyers who happened to share a body.

She sat in the last row of folding chairs near the voter check-in table, her brief spread across her knees, highlighters bleeding through the page. Around her, poll workers in name tags moved with the unhurried patience of people who had done this many times, and voters came and went in a slow, unremarkable procession that Emily found oddly steadying. An old man with a cane took eleven minutes at one booth. Nobody hurried him. She underlined a line from the majority opinion and thought about how easy it was to defend speech in the abstract, and how much harder it became the moment you imagined words doing actual damage.

Francois found her there, because of course he did; he had drawn the same case for the opposing side and had spent three days trying to convince her that the whole exercise was rigged. He dropped into the chair beside her, unwrapping a granola bar with the ceremony of someone postponing work. "You know the test they made up in Schenck is dead, right," he said. "Nobody uses it anymore. Later courts replaced it. You build your whole government argument on it and the panel will eat you alive."

"Mr. Costa said argue it as it was decided," Emily said. "Not as it aged."

"That's like arguing the earth is flat because someone once said so convincingly."

"No, it's like arguing what the test was, and whether it made sense, before anyone decided it didn't." She flipped to her second brief, the one for the socialists, and tapped the page. "And then I have to turn around and say the government was wrong to imprison a man for handing out leaflets. In an hour. With a straight face."

He chewed for a while. Behind them, a poll worker with a lugubrious voice was explaining to a young mother that she was at the wrong precinct, that her street fell three blocks short of this one, that she would have to drive across town before seven. The mother stood with a baby on her hip, absorbing the inconvenience without argument, and Emily watched her go and thought that most people most of the time accepted the rules they were handed. The socialists in the case had not, and the question that kept snagging her was whether their refusal had been courage or recklessness, and whether the answer changed depending on which side of the leaflet you stood.

"The test is called clear and present danger," Emily said, reading aloud, half to Francois and half to the folding chairs. "That's the phrase. The Court said speech could be punished if it created a clear and present danger of harm Congress could prevent." She said it twice more under her breath, testing the weight of it, because she had learned by now that if she could say a principle out loud without stumbling, she could defend it, even a principle she did not fully trust.

"That's the government's whole case in one sentence," Francois said. "Danger, clear, present, preventable. Four doors and you only have to walk through one."

"No, you have to walk through all four at once." She was surprising herself; she had not known she thought this until she said it. "That's the trap for the government too. Clear and present. Not dangerous someday, not dangerous in theory. If you reify the danger into some floating menace that might materialize, you've proven the socialists' point for them, that the government punishes fear instead of acts." She wrote in the margin of her brief, hard enough to tear the paper slightly, and decided she would open with that, whichever side she was on.

At the check-in table, a man in a delivery jacket was being told, gently, that he was registered under an old address, and there was a form he could fill out, and a phone number he could call if the form was rejected. Duress, Emily thought, was not only the threat of prison. It was the thousand small pressures that turned a right into an obstacle course, and she wondered whether the man would come back after his shift or whether the form would go into his truck and stay there, and this, too, felt like something the judges in her case had not had to think about, because they had been deciding about war and leaflets and not about Tuesday afternoons. She did not resolve it. She wrote duress in the margin and circled it, because she wanted to remember the feeling of not resolving it.

"Ten to three," Francois said, standing, balling up the granola wrapper. "Library. Alexa's saving us seats in the front so the panel can watch your face when you argue against yourself."

"Both of me are nervous," Emily said, and gathered her two briefs, one in each hand, the government's and the socialists', and held them apart like a scale as she walked out through the gymnasium doors into the ordinary daylight.

activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: The doctrine of double effect, traced to Thomas Aquinas, holds that causing a harm one foresees but does not intend can be permissible when it is a side effect of pursuing a good end.
story:
Isabella had the complaint email open on the library computer for the third day in a row, cursor blinking in the empty body of the message, when Harlow dropped into the chair beside her with a granola bar and no intention of leaving. The subject line read simply, Patient care, Ward 4, and Harlow leaned sideways to read it before Isabella could minimize the window.

"You're still on that," Harlow said. "It's been two weeks."

"It hasn't been two weeks. It's been eleven days." Isabella turned slightly in her seat, one hand resting on the mouse as though the gesture itself were an argument. "I heard what I heard."

What she had heard, standing outside Room 412 with a tray of untouched pudding cups, was the resident telling a nurse that the dose was right for the pain and that they weren't trying to hurry anything, and the nurse answering, quieter, that it might hurry it anyway. The old man inside had cancer in his spine and a daughter who visited on Sundays. Isabella had stood there with her tray and felt the door between her and something she didn't have words for, and then she had walked on, and the man had died four days later, and the daughter had sent a card to the ward thanking everyone. Isabella had read it twice at the nurses' station, looking for a clue about whether the daughter knew what the dose might have cost, and found nothing but cursive and gratitude.

Harlow peeled the wrapper off the granola bar. "You can't just dichotomize it," she said, crumbs and all. "Doctor bad, Isabella good, email sent, world fixed. That's not how any of this works."

"You think I don't know that?" But she said it without heat, because the truth was she had come to the library precisely because she didn't know how it worked. She had started with a search about medical ethics and reporting obligations, and the search had kept bending toward older questions, until late yesterday afternoon she had found a chapter that mentioned a doctrine traced to Thomas Aquinas. She read the page twice, then a third time. The doctrine of double effect held that causing a harm one foresaw but did not intend could be permissible when it came as a side effect of pursuing a good end. She copied the sentence into her notebook, and underneath it she wrote, but how do you know what anyone intends, and then she underlined that twice, which was as close as she had come to an answer.

Ms. Pérez found her there an hour before closing, reshelving nothing in particular, which was how Ms. Pérez conducted her rounds. "You've been in the ethics section all week," she said, tapping the stack beside Isabella's elbow. "College already?"

"Sort of." Isabella hesitated, then said it plainly, because Ms. Pérez had a way of standing there that made plainness feel possible. "The doctrine of double effect. Do you know it?"

Ms. Pérez's hand stilled on the stack for a moment, a small pause Isabella would not think about until later. "I know of it," she said. "It's an old argument. People have leaned on it for centuries, some honestly, some not." She slid a book back into its place on the shelf. "What's the essay question?"

"There isn't one. There's just a doctor." Isabella told it quickly, the tray, the dose, the four days, the card with the cursive. She left out that she had started the complaint email three times, though the computer screen behind her still had the subject line glowing at the top of it, and Ms. Pérez's eyes moved to it and back without comment. When Isabella finished, she heard her own uncertainty out loud for the first time and it sounded different than it had in her head. "The morphine might not even have been what shortened his life. He was sick in a dozen ways. The nurse said the other things could be confounders, that you couldn't separate them out."

"True," Ms. Pérez said. "And the harm, if there was harm, wasn't gratuitous. It wasn't cruelty for its own sake. That matters, or people have argued it matters since the thirteenth century." She picked up Isabella's notebook, glanced at the underlined question, and set it down again. "You may never answer that one. Intention is the hardest thing in the world to see from the outside."

Isabella nodded. She deleted the email that night, and she told herself it was a considered position, the doctrine and the confounders and the daughter's cursive all weighed together, and she also told herself she might simply have chosen the version that let her keep sleeping. She kept volunteering at the hospital on Saturdays. She requested Ward 4 without admitting to herself that she was requesting it.

It was Ms. Pérez she ran into in the hospital elevator in November, holding a bouquet of the cheap carnations they sold in the lobby. "My father," Ms. Pérez said, before Isabella could ask. "Room 412, back in the spring. I'm the one who wrote the card." The elevator doors opened on Four, and Ms. Pérez stepped out first, then turned. "He asked them, at the end. He said he didn't want to count the days if the days were going to hurt like that." She adjusted the carnations in her arm and walked toward the nurses' station, and the last thing Isabella heard her say was to the charge nurse, warm and unhesitating: "Is Dr. Okafor still on this floor? He was wonderful to my father."

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Most news articles use the 'inverted pyramid': the most important facts come first and less important details follow, so the opening paragraph carries the core story.
story:
The festival had spread itself across the town square in coloured awnings and folding tables, and Hayden found Mr. Popescu at the far corner, behind a stack of newspapers weighted with a kettle. Mr. Popescu had offered, back in June, to teach him enough Romanian to read the news, and Hayden had said yes mostly to have something to say when his grandmother asked what he was doing with his summer. Now it was August, and there was a table between them, and a folded paper, and no way out that did not involve admitting he had barely opened the workbook.

"Today you read," Mr. Popescu said. He unfolded the paper, turned past photographs of a flooded river and a handball match, and set his finger on a short article near the bottom of page four. "Aloud. Then you tell me what it says. In your own words, in Romanian, one minute."

Clara arrived before Hayden could begin. She was working the festival with a cooler of iced tea she had decided, that very morning, to monetize, three lei a cup, a laminated sign, a QR code her brother had printed at the library. She set two cups on the table without being asked, which Hayden understood as rent for the shade. She stayed, though. That part he had not budgeted for. She pulled a chair over and watched him with the frank patience of someone waiting to be entertained.

The first sentence nearly emptied him. He sounded out each word, checked the workbook's glossary, went back. Mr. Popescu corrected a vowel and said nothing else. By the end of the first paragraph Hayden had it: the mayor of a small town had resigned on Tuesday after the council rejected his budget. He kept going because stopping felt like quitting, and the second paragraph was about the council vote itself, and the third was a list of the mayor's previous positions, going back to a sports club in the nineties, and the fourth quoted a neighbour saying he was "not the worst man for the job," which Hayden recognized as litotes even before he could translate it, because Mr. Popescu used that same kind of praise on his own cooking. The last paragraph named the mayor's dog.

"One minute," Mr. Popescu said. "Summarise."

Hayden began with the dog. He had it freshest, having just decoded it, and he gave its name and the detail that it had been seen at the town hall, and only then did he circle back to the resignation, running out of Romanian halfway through and finishing in English. Clara laughed into her iced tea. Mr. Popescu did not laugh. He refolded the paper along its old creases and looked at the square, where a folk band was tuning behind them, badly.

"You read everything in order," he said. "Like a novel. But a news article is not a novel. It is an inverted pyramid. The most important facts come first, and the less important details follow, so the opening paragraph already carries the core story."

"That's why the dog was last," Hayden said.

"That is why the dog was last. If you have one minute, you read the first paragraph and you talk. If you have ten seconds, you read the first sentence." Mr. Popescu turned the paper around and slid it back. "Again. Do not read. Summarise what you already have."

Hayden tried it. The mayor, a small town, Tuesday, the budget rejected, the resignation. It came out crooked, with a wrong case ending on "mayor" and a long pause before "budget," but it came out, and when he finished, Clara put down her cup. "So the dog is just decoration," she said. "All that work for decoration." She seemed genuinely aggrieved on his behalf, though Hayden suspected the grievance was older than the dog, that it was about her sign, which had drawn four customers in two hours, all of them friends.

He thought about telling her the dog was not decoration exactly, that it told you something about the man that the budget figures did not, but that the pyramid was right anyway if you had only a minute. Both of those things could be true. What he could not settle was where the core of a person actually lived, in the resignation or in the dog, and he did not think the article settled it either. He said none of this. Instead he counted out coins for the iced tea, and Clara swept them into the cooler's coin pouch, and Mr. Popescu folded the paper in half, in half again, and tucked it under the kettle for tomorrow.

"One more," he said, and turned to a fresh page.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: In Texas v. Johnson (1989), the Supreme Court ruled 5-4 that burning the American flag as a political protest is protected symbolic speech.
story:
David had drawn the side he didn't believe in. Ms. Huang slid the assignment sheet across the reference desk and watched his face as he read it: petitioner, State of Texas, respondent Gregory Lee Johnson. His job was to argue that burning the flag could be punished. He wanted to argue the other side, and he said so.

"That's the point," Ms. Huang said. "Anyone can win the argument they already like." She pointed him toward the law stacks, third floor, where the reporters sat in dull green bindings.

He found Texas v. Johnson in the 1989 volume and read the headnote twice before it settled. The Supreme Court had ruled, five votes to four, that burning the American flag as a political protest was protected symbolic speech. Five to four. He copied the line into his notebook and then sat very still, because five to four meant that one justice, a single person, had stood between Johnson and a prison cell. The side he thought was obvious had almost won.

Colin was already at the back table with his laptop open, which meant Colin had drawn the respondent, the winning side, the fun side. "I've got Brennan," Colin said when David sat down. "The government can't prohibit expression just because society finds the idea offensive. It writes itself."

"Mine doesn't write itself," David said. "Mine has to say the flag isn't just speech, it's the thing speech happens under." Even as he verbalized it, he heard how thin it sounded next to Colin's quotation, and he hated how much he liked Colin's quotation.

They practiced cross-examinations on each other all week. Cyril, who had been assigned to judge, sat between them with a legal pad and an expression of performative boredom. "Objection," Cyril kept saying. "This is facetious." It wasn't, usually, but Cyril liked the word, and it had a certain force when David tried cheap tricks, like implying that Johnson had wanted a riot rather than a response. The cheap tricks worked on Cyril. That was the part that scared him. If Cyril could be moved by rhetoric he knew was dishonest, the argument didn't need to be true to win, and David felt the pull of that the way you feel a current under a calm surface.

The night before the mock court, David stayed until the closing announcement. Ms. Huang was reshelving near the elevator, and he asked her the question he couldn't shake. "If it was five to four, doesn't that mean the Court basically flipped a coin? Like the answer wasn't there and they just voted their guts?"

"Or," she said, not pausing in her shelving, "it means the two answers were both defensible and they had to choose. Close cases aren't coin flips. They're the ones worth arguing."

He walked home carrying that sentence alongside the other one, five to four, and they sat next to each other without merging. He tried to write his closing argument and found he was writing two speeches, one for each side, and neither would let the other finish.

In the gymnasium the next afternoon, folding chairs stood in for the bench, and Cyril wore his father's gray blazer and looked sufficiently judicial to make people straighten up. Colin went first and was good, fluid, principled. Then David stood, and instead of the speech he'd drafted, he gave the one he'd found. He said the flag was unique, that it stood for the very right being used against it, and that a nation could honor that right and still say this one object is different. He believed maybe sixty percent of it, and he argued it better than anything he'd ever believed completely. Watching Cyril lean forward, David understood that the mendacity, if that's what it was, lived not in the argument but in the seam between it and himself, and that he could not locate the seam exactly, not even now.

Cyril ruled for Johnson, five to four, having recruited two classmates to vote with him. Afterward Colin clapped David's shoulder and said, "You almost had me." David gathered his notes, both sets of them, the one he'd given and the one he'd buried, and outside the gym the flag on the pole caught the wind and snapped once, twice, and he stood there watching it until the bus came.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: During China's Qingming Festival, which falls on April 4, 5 or 6, families visit their ancestors' graves to sweep and clean them and leave offerings of food.
story:
The morning of the burial, Xavier discovered his grandmother packing a plastic bag with oranges, a tin of shortbread, and a whisk broom, and he assumed grief had done something strange to her mind. They had buried no one yet. The coffin was still at the funeral home, and here she was with food, as if for a picnic, in the back of his aunt's car.

"You'll want the broom later," she said, and would say nothing else about it.

His grandfather had been the loquacious one, the one who talked through entire dinners about the Hangchow of his boyhood, the rain, the fish markets, the aunt who proselytized about every diet she tried and ruined every New Year with it. Xavier, who at twelve had found these monologues unbearable, had at seventeen begun recording them on his phone until his grandfather noticed and performed for the microphone, exaggerating, making even the rain sound operatic. The last recording was four minutes long. It cut off mid-sentence because a nurse had come in with medication.

At the cemetery the service was short and correct and cold for April. Xavier had had a presentiment all week that he would embarrass himself by crying at the wrong moment, and instead he embarrassed himself by not crying at all, which felt worse, a dryness he kept touching like a missing tooth. Daniela, who had driven two hours from her college visit to stand beside him, squeezed his elbow and whispered, "Your tie is crooked," which was her way of saying everything else. Ryley texted him a single thumbs-up, having determined that funerals were beyond his social range, and Xavier had laughed, alone in the bathroom, at the honesty of it.

After the crowd thinned, his grandmother led him back up the hill to the raw rectangle of earth. She took out the whisk broom and handed it to him. "Your grandfather would want you to do this," she said. "Not today, exactly. Today we just show you."

"Show me what?"

She crouched, old knees complaining, and brushed grit from the temporary marker. "Every spring. April fourth, fifth, sixth, somewhere in there, that's when it falls. Qingming. Families visit their ancestors' graves. We sweep, we clean, we leave food." She set an orange on the stone like a small bright argument. "He did it for his mother in her cemetery in Oakland for thirty years. You never came because you were at school, and he never made it a lesson. He just went."

Xavier stood holding the broom, understanding slowly that his grandfather's stories had not been stories only but maintenance, a grave swept with words. He had thought the visits ended when the person ended; that was the arithmetic he had grown up with, one funeral, one goodbye, then memory left to fend for itself. His grandmother had a different accounting, in which the dead were visited, fed, tidied after, treated less like a finished chapter and more like a relative who had simply moved somewhere with poor phone service.

"Oranges," Xavier said. "He liked the shortbread better."

"He did." She smiled with half her mouth. "So leave the shortbread and I'll take the oranges home. He'd hate for the birds to get the good tin."

He set the tin down beside her orange, and she laughed at his solemnity, the way he placed it like an offering at an altar rather than a biscuit on the ground, and he laughed too, and the laughing cracked something open so that his eyes finally stung, and he was grateful to the shortbread for it. Daniela waited by the car with her hands in her pockets, not hurrying him.

He could not decide, walking down the hill, whether he believed his grandfather received anything, whether the food was a message or just a way of making the hands do what the mouth no longer could. He decided he would come next April anyway, broom and oranges and the good tin, and let the belief arrive or not arrive in its own time. His grandmother took his arm on the gravel path. "You'll come," she said, not a question, and he said, "I'll come," and opened the car door for her, the broom still in his hand, which she noticed and said nothing about.

fact: In Mahanoy Area School District v. B.L. (2021), the Supreme Court ruled 8-1 that a school violated a student's free speech by punishing an off-campus Snapchat post.
story:
The kitchen table had become a war room by ten o'clock: two stacks of index cards, one labeled SCHOOL and one labeled STUDENT, and between them a laptop open to a database Jacob had never used before. His mother had gone to bed with a reminder that the porch light stayed on, and the house had settled into its diurnal exhale, the refrigerator humming, the furnace ticking through its cycles. He was supposed to argue both sides of a free speech case before the mock court on Thursday, and so far he had argued neither one well.

"Read me what you have," Haylie said from the laptop's speakers, her voice tinny over the video call. She was doing her own brief across town, but she liked to hear his out loud, the way a musician plays a passage for someone else to catch the false notes.

"The school has a duty to maintain order," Jacob recited. "Speech that disrupts the learning environment can be regulated, and schools don't stop being schools at the property line." He paused. "Then I have to stand up, walk around the table, and say the opposite."

"That's the assignment, yes."

He picked up a card from the student stack and read it again, though he already knew it by heart. It was the case Kailey had flagged for him that afternoon in the library, the one she'd found in fifteen minutes after he'd spent two days circling the question of off-campus speech like a dog afraid of the bath. She'd slid her laptop across the table without a word, just the case name printed at the top, and gone back to her biology notes.

"Wait, I already told you this," Haylie said. "Mahanoy Area School District versus B.L. Tell me what it says."

"In 2021, the Supreme Court ruled eight to one that a school violated a student's free speech by punishing an off-campus Snapchat post," Jacob said. He heard himself say it slowly, like a person checking the ice before stepping on it. Eight to one. Even the justices who usually disagreed had agreed on this.

"So your student side is strong."

"That's the problem. It's so strong that I can't find the school's best argument. And Mr. Nielsen wants both sides to instantiate the principle, not just assert it. His word. He said a claim that never meets a real example is just noise."

Haylie laughed at that, because it sounded exactly like Mr. Nielsen, who taught civics as though the Constitution were a living thing with moods. Then she said something that stopped him. "Why did you pick this case, anyway? You had a list of options. Three of them were easier."

The furnace ticked. Outside, a car passed on the wet street, its tires making that long sighing sound, and Jacob watched its headlights travel across the index cards. He had chosen the case quickly, too quickly, on Monday morning, before he had read a single brief.

"Because it's current," he said.

"You're a bad liar over video. I can see your face."

He looked at the school stack, then at his phone, face down beside the laptop since dinner. On Saturday night, at Kailey's bonfire, he had made a post. It was a Snapchat, meant to vanish, a joke at the expense of a coach who had cut him from the team that afternoon, the kind of joke that was funny for exactly as long as nobody with authority saw it. On Monday, a teammate had texted him a screenshot of it, no message attached. Then Mr. Nielsen had handed out the mock court topics, and Jacob had taken the off-campus speech case before anyone else could, a move that now struck him as something between research and camouflage.

"Somebody screenshotted something I posted," he said. "I don't know who has it."

Haylie was quiet long enough that he checked whether the call had dropped. "Do you think it's a synchronicity?" she asked. "The case and your post showing up the same week?"

"No. I think it's Monday morning and I got lucky." Though even as he said it, he understood it wasn't luck, that he had chosen the case the way a person chooses an umbrella after getting wet. He pulled the laptop closer and typed the case name into the search bar again, not to reread it but to see it one more time, eight to one, the school in the wrong, the student vindicated. The holding was clear. What was not clear was anything about his own situation: whether a screenshot still counted as an off-campus post, whether a joke was disruption, whether a coach who hadn't said a word to him was already past saying words.

"Here's your school-side argument," Haylie said. "Argue it against yourself. Argue it knowing you're the student. That's how you make it honest."

Jacob stood, took the school stack, and began pacing the kitchen the way he would on Thursday, testing the rhythm of it. "The school has a duty," he said to the dark window, "to protect the conditions under which every student can learn." It sounded better out loud. It also sounded, for the first time, like something that could be aimed at him.

He picked up his phone and turned it over.

"Jacob," Haylie said, "just tell me what the post said."

"It said the coach couldn't find the sideline with both hands," he said, and, waiting, he set the phone down again, face up this time.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Methane traps far more heat per molecule than carbon dioxide, but a methane molecule stays in the atmosphere for only about a decade on average, much less time than carbon dioxide.
story:
The quarry behind Brianna's backyard had gone quiescent for the season, its machinery parked in rows along the far wall, so the only sound on Saturday afternoon was the pool filter and Rory flipping pages of her printed graphs with an impatience that made the paper snap.

"You're saying it wrong," Rory said. "Keeling. It's pronounced like 'keyling,' not 'keeling.' It's in the phonetics."

"It's a name, not a vocabulary word." Brianna looked at the graph anyway: carbon dioxide climbing from a wobble around 310 to a smooth, unbroken rise past 400, a hockey stick with a long handle. Below it she had taped a second graph, methane, which needed magnifying at the recent end, and between the two she had spread her notes, which she was supposed to collate into one coherent explanation by Monday. The scholarship committee hadn't asked for a lecture. They had asked each finalist to explain, in plain language, how greenhouse gases trap heat, and to read a century of carbon dioxide off a chart, and Brianna had discovered that explaining something simply was harder than understanding it.

"So walk me through it," Rory said, lying back on the picnic table. "Pretend I'm a rich person who doesn't believe in anything."

"Sunlight comes through the atmosphere and warms the ground, and the ground radiates heat back up as infrared, and greenhouse gases absorb that outgoing heat and re-emit it, some of it downward, so the surface stays warmer than it would otherwise."

"That was decent. Now the graph."

"Here, the sawtooth before 1960 is seasonal, plants breathing, and it flattens because there weren't enough stations, and then it just goes up. It never levels off. That's the part I want them to feel. It doesn't pause."

"Okay, but here's my thing." Rory sat up, which she always did right before an argument. "The cement plant. My mom's petition is about the quarry's methane leaks, and my uncle says it's a waste of time, that methane is nothing compared to CO2, that the petition should target the CO2 or it's dishonest. Who's right?"

"Your uncle," Brianna said, almost immediately, because she had spent two weeks with these graphs and the carbon dioxide line was the one that never stopped. "CO2 is the main driver. It accumulates. That's the whole story of the last century."

"Except my chemistry teacher said methane traps way more heat per molecule than CO2. Like, way more. So isn't it worse?"

"That can't be both ways. If methane is so much stronger, why does everyone talk about carbon dioxide?"

They were quiet for a second. The filter hummed. From over the fence came the sound of Mr. Ma watering his tomatoes, which he did every evening at five, and which meant he had heard everything they'd said for the past hour, because sound carried strangely between the yards, the quarry wall bouncing it back.

"Per molecule," Brianna said slowly.

"What?"

"Per molecule. Stronger per molecule. But it matters how long the stuff stays up there. Look at this." She pulled the methane sheet out from under the others and found the lifespan column, running her finger down it. "A methane molecule stays in the atmosphere about a decade on average. A carbon dioxide molecule stays much longer. So if you stop the leaks, the methane that's already up there goes away relatively soon."

Rory frowned at the page. "So cutting methane would actually slow warming faster. In the next few years. Because it clears out."

"And CO2 just keeps accumulating, so it's the long game." Brianna sat back on the bench. "I said your uncle was right."

"You did."

"I was wrong. I had it exactly backwards. The strong one is the fast one, and the weak one is the permanent one."

"That's a terrible slogan," Rory said, "but yes."

"I've been telling people for a month that methane barely matters because there's less of it. I told that to Julie. I told it with confidence."

"Julie agrees with everything you say. That's not data."

"Shut up. Bring me the hose, I'm watering the impatiens while I think." She took the hose and stood there not watering anything, holding the nozzle, watching the graphs curl slightly in the heat on the table. The honest version, she was realizing, was not one gas or the other. Methane cuts bought speed; carbon dioxide cuts bought permanence; the petition and the century-scale line on the graph were both true at once, and the only dishonest thing would be pretending the tension wasn't there. She would have to say that to the committee, out loud, and admit she had gotten it backwards two weeks ago, which cost her something to imagine.

"Excuse me," Mr. Ma said over the fence, still holding his watering can. "So which one should the petition be about? I only heard the second half."
