"Both," Brianna said. "Methane first, for the next few years. But your uncle's not wrong about the long run, whoever he is."

"My uncle is my uncle," Rory said. "He drives a truck."

Mr. Ma considered this, then tipped his can over the last tomato. "Then I will sign both," he said, and Brianna turned the nozzle on the impatiens at last, the water arcing gold in the low sun.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: The phrase 'rule of thirds' was first written down by John Thomas Smith in his 1797 book Remarks on Rural Scenery.
story:
The paint cans were lined up on the grass like witnesses, and Maika had until six o'clock, when her grandmother's retirement party would spill out of the house and into the yard. Three hours, and the back fence was still a blank gray expanse waiting for the mural she had promised: the lake where her grandmother had grown up, the water her grandmother described every time anyone asked about home. Maika had drawn the lake a dozen times on paper. On paper it behaved. On eight feet of weathered cedar it refused.

Lia arrived at four carrying brushes and two bottles of iced tea, and stood in the grass with her head tilted. "Put the horizon a third of the way down," she said. "Rule of thirds. Off center is better."

Maika loaded a roller and considered the fence as if it owed her money. "Who made that a rule?"

"Some dead painter, probably." Lia shrugged. "I don't know. Ms. Farah told us at the studio. All I remember is the horizon goes a third down, and the important thing sits on a third line, not in the middle."

The problem was that Maika had been planning the lake dead center, because that was how it lived in her grandmother's stories: the whole of it, held in the middle of every telling. Moving it felt like a small betrayal. But the sketch taped to the porch railing showed a plump, symmetrical painting, polite and inert, the kind of thing that hangs in a dentist's office. She had painted what the lake meant instead of what it looked like, and the two were not the same.

"The center's safe," she said, mostly to herself. "Everybody can find the center."

"Safe is boring," Lia said, and opened a bottle of tea with her shirt hem.

They painted the sky first, a blue that leaned toward evening, and Maika measured the cedar boards with her thumb to find the third mark and laid the horizon there, low, the way the lake actually sat under all that open Polish sky. The water took the bottom third. Something about the proportion made her breath catch; the fence had become a window instead of a picture. She worked fast, the deadline pressing on her like duress, sweat gluing hair to her neck, and she did not stop to equivocate about the shoreline anymore. She let it run ragged.

At half past five Matthias climbed over the side gate, which was unnecessary and entirely like him, holding his phone. "I looked it up," he announced. "You asked who made the rule. It was a guy named John Thomas Smith. He first wrote the phrase down in 1797, in a book called Remarks on Rural Scenery."

"That's a real title?" Lia said.

"That's a real title." Matthias turned the phone around so they could see the old engraved cover. "So it's not, like, a law of physics. It's one man's opinion that got repeated for two hundred years."

Maika stood back from the fence, roller dripping onto the grass, and felt the ground shift slightly under her certainty. If the rule was only an opinion, then following it was a choice, not obedience. And if it was a choice, then she had chosen it, and that was different from being told. She thought of her own drawings, all those centered horizons, and realized she had been treating habit as if it were principle. Maybe rules were just other people's decisions that you either inherited or didn't. She could not settle the whole question standing in wet paint, and she was honest enough with herself to admit that.

"There's a birch on the shore," she said. "In the stories there's always a birch." She pointed to the left third of the fence, where a vertical line would catch the eye. "There. Not the middle."

"Epicurean of you," Matthias said, examining the iced tea she handed him. "This is the good stuff."

"It's from my grandmother's pantry. She has opinions about tea."

Maika painted the birch quickly, white trunk, a few decisive branches, and stood back again. The lake lay low and wide, the tree leaning toward the water from the third line, and the whole composition had a tension that her centered sketches had never managed. It was not finished. The far shore needed trees, the water needed light, and she had forty minutes. But it was already more alive than anything she had made on paper, and she knew part of that was the proportion and part of it was that she had chosen it herself, on purpose, after asking who had chosen first.

The screen door banged and her grandmother came out in her good dress, hands folded, appraising. She looked at the fence for a long moment while the three of them held their brushes like guilty suspects.

"The water," her grandmother said finally, "was never so calm."

Maika picked up the roller and broke the surface with a long diagonal of gray.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: According to the CDC, wearing a seat belt reduces serious crash-related injuries and deaths by about half.
story:
The car smelled like vanilla air freshener and, underneath that, like every nervous teenager who had ever gripped its wheel. Jason sat in the driver's seat of his father's sedan with his hands at ten and two, the way Mr. Buchanan had instructed, and waited for something to happen. In the back seat, Kieran was already filming.

"Say something to the camera," Kieran said. "First words of a licensed driver."

"I don't have a license. That's the entire point of today."

Mr. Buchanan settled into the passenger seat with the unhurried gravity of a man who had done this four thousand times and expected to do it four thousand more. He was a neighbour from two doors down, retired from something no one had ever specified, and he charged twenty dollars an hour in cash. He put on his own seat belt, clicked it, and looked at Vanessa, who was sitting behind him with her phone out.

"Seat belt," he said.

"I'm in the back."

"Belt."

Vanessa sighed the sigh of someone being asked to observe an obsolete custom, but she reached for it. Jason watched her in the mirror. The strap was twisted and she didn't fix it; she just draped the thing over her shoulder like a scarf and went back to her phone. Mr. Buchanan folded his arms.

"We're not starting the lesson," he said.

"Because of the belt?" Vanessa held it up as evidence. "I'm wearing it."

"You're wearing it wrong, and we're not moving until it's right." He said it the way you'd announce rain, no heat in it at all, which somehow made it worse. Kieran lowered his camera, sensing material.

"That's so gratuitous," Vanessa said. "We haven't even left the driveway."

Jason had read something about this, and now it surfaced the way facts did, arriving without their sources attached. He'd been scrolling two nights ago, avoiding a college essay prompt about a challenge he'd overcome, and he'd found a page from the CDC. Wearing a seat belt cut serious crash-related injuries and deaths by about half. Not a little. Half. He'd kept scrolling at the time, but the number had stayed with him, the way certain numbers did, taking up residence without paying rent.

"He's right," Jason said, and everyone turned to him, which he hadn't planned for. "I read it. The CDC. Belts reduce serious crash-related injuries and deaths by about half. Like, in half. Half of them."

"Injuries and deaths," Mr. Buchanan repeated, nodding slowly, as if confirming a rumor he himself had started.

"That's one page on the internet," Vanessa said. "You believe everything you read?"

"Actually," Kieran said from the back, with the delight of a man delivering a checkmate, "that's a very interesting question of epistemology. How do you know anything, Ness? You believe the weather app. You believed Kelsey when she said the calc test got moved."

"That was different."

"It was identical."

While they argued, Jason looked at the twisted strap in the mirror and thought about the fact from both directions at once, which was a habit his mother called overthinking and his father called being careful. On one hand, the statistic was abstract, a population-level average that had nothing to do with this driveway, this car, this afternoon; half of a number he'd never be. On the other hand, the strap was right there, twisted, a five-second fix, and the cost of fixing it was nothing. He couldn't prove the fact applied to Vanessa specifically. He couldn't prove it didn't. But the asymmetry was so lopsided it felt less like a decision and more like arithmetic.

"Can I just?" He unbuckled, twisted around over his shoulder, grabbed the strap behind Vanessa, and untwisted it with one pull. She let him, mostly out of surprise. He rebuckled his own belt and put his hands back at ten and two.

Vanessa looked at the now-flat strap lying across her chest, then at her phone, then, for a moment, at nothing in particular. She clicked the buckle tighter without being asked.

Mr. Buchanan started the engine.

"Hands at ten and two," he said, "and pull out slowly. There's a mailbox on your left that has survived every student I've ever taught. Let's keep the streak alive."

Jason checked the mirror, signalled, and eased them down the driveway, past the mailbox, its paint flaking but its post perfectly straight, into the street.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: The dependency ratio compares people aged under 15 and 65 and over with people aged 15 to 64, estimating how many dependents each working-age person supports.
story:
The departure board said DELAYED in the amber letters that airports habituate you to trusting, and Alexander spread his geography notes across two seats at Gate 14 while his mother queued at the coffee cart with their last bills before the currency exchange. He was supposed to be on a school trip to Lisbon, a conference on demographics that Mr. Almeida had talked up for a semester, and now the whole group sat scattered around the gate like spilled counters. His exam was in nine days. The population pyramid printed on his page was shaped like a barrel, wide at the top, narrow at the base, and he could not decide what it meant for the country it described.

Mikayla dropped into the seat across from him and stole his water bottle. "You're doing the pyramid thing."

"I'm failing the pyramid thing." He turned the page sideways, as though the country would look different lying down. "I can describe it. Wide top, that's old people. Narrow base, few kids. But then the question asks what the government should build, schools or nursing homes, and I just write both and feel like a dilettante."

Izak leaned over from the next row, headphones half off. "It's a trick question. You build schools either way because kids pay taxes later."

"Not for twenty years," Mikayla said. "Not one of those kids supports anyone for twenty years."

"Neither do old people," Izak said.

"That's the point, though." Alexander pulled the page toward himself again, defensive, because Izak had a way of making him feel wrong before he'd even finished. "The old people already did their supporting. That's what I can't get straight. Who carries whom, right now, and how much."

His mother came back with two coffees and sat down beside him, and she was still holding the receipt, frowning at it, when she said that the airport tax alone had gone up since last year, that everything kept going up, and that she'd like to know who exactly was supposed to pay for it all.

"You are," Alexander said, before he thought about it.

"Excuse me."

"Workers. People aged 15 to 64." He was talking faster now, half surprised at himself, tapping the pyramid. "Look. There's a thing called the dependency ratio. It compares people under 15 and people 65 and over against people aged 15 to 64, and it estimates how many dependents each working-age person supports." The sentence came out whole, textbook-smooth, and his mother set the coffee down.

"So in this country," she said, "each of me is carrying how many of them."

"That's what I have to work out." He counted along the bars with his pen, the wide top heavy with 70-to-74s, the base so thin the 0-to-4 bar barely registered. In a place shaped like this, every worker had more dependents above than below. More nursing homes than schools. He wrote it in the margin and underlined nothing, because Izak was watching.

Izak shrugged. "So old people are a burden. Nice."

"I didn't say burden." Alexander heard how it had sounded, and it sat wrong with him. His grandmother had raised Izak's little sister for two years while Izak's parents worked; everyone at school knew that. "I said dependent. It's just who's not counted as working-age. A retiree who babysits every day still lands on the wrong side of the line."

"Then the line's stupid."

"Maybe the line's just a line," Mikayla said. "Maybe you build the nursing homes and the schools, and the ratio tells you how to split the budget."

Mr. Almeida came back from the service desk with news, and it cut the argument off mid-breath: the flight wasn't going tonight, the airline was putting them in a hotel near the perimeter road, and the conference's opening session would be over before any of them landed. Nine days to the exam and a night in a hotel with a pool he wouldn't use. Alexander closed his notes while everyone gathered bags, and his mother asked, quietly, whether the ratio worked the other way too, whether a country full of children could squeeze the workers just as hard. He said yes, that it could, that he hadn't worked out which was worse, and that he suspected nobody had.

They rode the shuttle to the hotel in the dark, the runway lights strobing past, and Izak fell asleep against the window with his mouth open, and Mikayla texted someone, and Alexander held the pyramid page on his knee without reading it. At the hotel desk the clerk apologised twice, assigned them rooms, and then asked for ID, and it turned out that everyone under 18 needed an adult signature for the night, one adult per minor, and there were six of them and only two adults from the school. Mr. Almeida counted them off on his fingers, twice, and looked at the clerk, and the clerk looked at the clock, and Alexander, watching two teachers prepare to argue over who would be responsible for whom, took out his pen and started to draw a pyramid of his own on the back of the boarding pass.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: A Sikh gurdwara's langar serves free vegetarian meals to anyone regardless of religion, caste or status, and people traditionally eat together seated on the floor as equals.
story:
The parking lot of the gurdwara was already full when Morgan's mother circled it twice, narrating her despair like a documentary voiceover. "Vaisakhi," she kept saying, "everyone comes for Vaisakhi," as though Morgan had not been the one to suggest it, and as though Morgan had not, in a moment of either bravery or lunacy, invited Graydon along.

Graydon was unfolding himself from the back seat, all elbows and questions. "So is there like a dress code? Because I'm wearing my grandpa's funeral shirt, which feels wrong on multiple levels."

"Cover your head," Morgan said, handing him a scarf from the bag her mother kept for exactly this purpose, for guests who showed up unprepared and slightly panicked. "And take your shoes off inside. And don't ask me anything else until we're through the door, because I'm nervous enough."

"You're nervous? You've been coming here since you were a fetus."

"I've never brought anyone," Morgan said, and then, because that sounded more sentimental than she intended, "anyone who asks this many questions."

Inside, the hall smelled of cardamom and hot oil and the particular sweetness of halved oranges. An uncle in a bright turban pressed steel cups of chai into their hands before Morgan could explain that they hadn't done anything to deserve it yet. They walked through the darbar hall, bowed where her mother bowed, stood through the kirtan while Graydon whispered that the harmonium player was "objectively shredding," which Morgan chose to accept as reverence.

Then came the langar hall, and this was the part Morgan had described in the car, badly, in a rush: the free meal, everyone seated in rows on the floor, and the fact that the food was vegetarian and served to anyone, whatever your religion or caste or status. She had tried to say it like it was a nice logistical detail. Graydon stopped in the doorway.

"Hold on. Anyone? Like, a random person off the street could walk in and eat?"

"That's the whole point," Morgan said. "Everyone sits on the floor together. Nobody's up on a throne."

"That's either communism or the nicest thing I've ever heard."

"It's langar," said a woman with a ladle, without looking up from the dal, and Graydon, chastened by a single word, sat down.

They ate with their palms cupped like everyone else's, and Morgan watched Graydon have what she could only call an experience. He got seconds of the kheer. He tried to give the serving uncle a tip, which nearly caused a diplomatic incident, and afterward he lay his palm over his heart and said, "I want to be clear that I would fight someone for this rice pudding, and I also want to be clear that fighting is against the rules here, which I respect."

Somewhere between the roti and the kheer, Gia materialized across the row, having arrived late with her own family, and leaned over with the expression of someone collecting gossip for later distribution. "Is that Graydon? Did you bring Graydon to Vaisakhi?"

"He invited himself, basically."

"I did not," Graydon said. "I was lured. With promises I now realize were undersold."

Gia's eyebrows conducted an entire conversation on their own. Gia's family, Morgan knew, had spent the past year in a slow-burning argument about whether she could go to a friend's church, a synagogue, a mosque, whether looking at other traditions from the inside was curiosity or corrosion. Morgan had watched Gia defend it with a cerebral, careful logic that never quite defeated her grandmother's blunt injunction: we do not go. We just don't. And here sat Gia, on the floor of her own gurdwara, watching Morgan's friend eat their food with his shoes off and his grandfather's funeral shirt going soft at the collar, and Morgan understood, in a way she hadn't before, that Gia's grandmother and Gia were both afraid of the same thing from opposite directions. Whether a person could walk into another room and still come back out the same.

Her mother settled cross-legged beside them with a plate she had no intention of finishing, since finishing was not the point of her plate. "Morgan, your phuphi wants to know if your friend has a grandmother who cooks."

"Tell her his grandmother only makes toast," Graydon said solemnly. "Burnt toast. I've been malnourished my whole life. Nobody at school understands. They vilify me for my packed lunches."

"Nobody vilifies you for your lunches," Morgan said.

"Jocelyn once called my sandwich a war crime."

Gia had gone quiet, watching the rows fill, the aunties moving down the lines with buckets of dal, the whole machinery of feeding strangers. When she spoke it was almost to the floor. "Do you think it counts, if you only ever host? Like, is it real if you never go anywhere else?"

Morgan turned her spoon over, buying time with it. She had an answer shaped like yes, of course, and another shaped like probably not, and they were both true, and neither of them was hers to hand out like a cup of chai.

"I think," she said slowly, "that the whole design of this room is that you can't tell who's hosting and who's visiting. That might be the point. Or it might be a coincidence. I'm still working on it."

Gia nodded, unsatisfied, which was fair.

Later, in the parking lot, shoes back on, scarf returned, Graydon stopped by the donation box and fed it a five with the ceremony of a man planting a flag. "For the rice pudding army," he explained.

"You can't buy your way into heaven," Morgan said.

"I'm not trying to get into heaven. I'm trying to get invited back."

Her mother unlocked the car, and Gia jogged out after them, breathless, phone in hand, saying that her grandmother wanted to know whether Graydon's family had anyone unmarried, and would he like to come to dinner next month.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: Translation usually begins at the codon AUG, which also codes for the amino acid methionine.
story:
Aiden spread the flashcards across the picnic table before the sun dropped behind the fence, because the fair was tomorrow and his model was still wrong somewhere. The backyard smelled of cut grass and the charcoal his father had left cooling by the grill, and Walker sat on the table's edge spinning a lacrosse ball on one finger while Leif read the instructions for the third time.

"Your mRNA strip says AUGCAUGCAUGCAUG," Leif said, holding the paper strip up to the light. "That's it. That's the whole puzzle."

"Then it should be easy," Aiden said, laying out his codon chart. "Three letters at a time. C A U, G C A, U G C." He wrote the amino acids beneath each group and frowned at them, because the list made no chain at all, just a stutter of the same few names.

Walker leaned over, sardonic as ever. "Congratulations, you've invented protein gibberish. They'll give you a ribbon for that."

Leif tapped the strip with one finger. "Maybe you're cutting it in the wrong place. Like, if you start on the second letter instead of the first, you get U G C, A U G, C A U. Different words." She slid the paper toward him, and Aiden went still, because she was right about the cutting and wrong about where to cut, or maybe the opposite, and he couldn't yet tell which.

He pulled out his phone and found the worksheet Ms. Martínez had handed back on Friday, the one with the red circle around his first attempt. At the bottom, in her narrow handwriting, was a note that had felt like a subpoena when he first read it, summoning him to figure out what he'd done wrong on his own time: Begin at AUG. He looked at the strip, found the A, and cut from there. A U G, C A U, G C A, U G. The first word gave him methionine, and after that the chain assembled itself, short but real, an actual protein hiding inside what had looked like noise.

"Translation usually begins at the codon AUG," Leif said, reading from the textbook chapter open on her knee. "It also codes for methionine. So every one of these strips probably starts with it. That's like a you-are-here marker." She wasn't explaining it to him, exactly; she was thinking out loud, testing the idea against the strip in his hand, and the difference mattered to Aiden even if he couldn't have said why.

Walker tossed the lacrosse ball against the garage door, catching it without looking. "So the fair judges are going to hand kids these strips, and the kids who start at the wrong letter get garbage, and the ones who find the AUG get a protein."

"That's the game, yeah." Aiden copied the corrected chain onto his display board, and the letters catalyzed something in his memory, the way Ms. Martínez had said concepts do when they finally connect. He understood the copying part too, roughly, how the cell reads DNA and writes the message out in RNA before the little machine reads the message again and builds. What he still couldn't answer was why it worked that way, why this code and not another, and he decided he would put that question on the board in his own handwriting and let a judge sit with it, the way he was sitting with it now.

Later, after Leif had gone home and Walker had taken the ball inside, Aiden's phone buzzed on the table. A message from Leif: "Tried my brother's strip. Started at the wrong end first, got nonsense, then flipped it and found the AUG second letter in. The marker can be hiding anywhere. Also my mom says good luck tomorrow." He read it twice, then texted Ms. Martínez a single line: I found where to start. She replied with a thumbs-up and nothing else, which somehow felt like the most anyone had trusted him all week.

He gathered the flashcards before the mosquitoes came out, stacked them against the board, and weighted the whole thing with the bag of charcoal so the wind off the prairie wouldn't take it in the night. Then he stood in the dark backyard looking at the strip of paper still pinned to the display, AUGCAUGCAUGCAUG, and read it one last time, beginning where the message began.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: According to the CDC, US drivers aged 16 to 19 have a fatal crash rate almost three times as high as drivers aged 20 and older, per mile driven.
story:
The waiting room of the licensing office smelled like hand sanitizer and old carpet, and Mathis sat between Colin and a wall he could not stop reading. Above the plastic chairs, in letters designed to be unmissable, a poster said that drivers aged 16 to 19 had a fatal crash rate almost three times as high as drivers aged 20 and older, per mile driven. He read it twice, then a third time, because the first two readings felt like a personal accusation.

"Natalie's going to love that," Colin said, nodding at the poster. "She failed her permit test twice. She says the whole system exists to stigmatize teenagers." Colin's own permit, earned on the first try, sat in his wallet like a trophy he was too polite to mention and too proud not to. He wanted, more than anything, to be the first of them with a license, the one who drove everyone to the lake in his mother's borrowed car, and he had appointed himself the group's expert on all things automotive since roughly Tuesday.

Natalie came back from the test window holding her results slip like a fish she had caught. "Passed," she announced. "Third attempt. I'd like the record to show that the examiner winked at me." She dropped into the chair on Mathis's other side, saw where he was looking, and read the poster aloud in a news-anchor voice. "Fatal crash rate almost three times as high as drivers twenty and older, per mile driven. Per mile, Mathis. So it's not even that we drive badly, it's that we drive badly efficiently."

"It's per mile so it's fair," Colin said. "You can't say teens crash more just because teens drive more." He said it the way he said everything, with the confidence of a boy who had once assembled a bookshelf without the instructions. Mathis privately tested the sentence against the poster and found it held. The comparison had already done the dividing. It was three times per mile, which meant three times even after you accounted for how little he actually drove, which was, so far, zero miles, a record he was about to ruin.

At the desk, a woman with reading glasses on a chain gave him a clipboard. "First lesson today? With Nowak? Lucky you. He's the one who doesn't yell." She said this as though the others were a menu option. His phone buzzed in his pocket, and under the desk, where the clipboard could not see, he read a message from his mother: I know you're nervous. Your grandfather didn't drive until he was 31 and he turned out fine, mostly. Text me after. Do not text during. Love, Mom. The comma after "fine" had somehow contained an entire childhood of being watched and worried over, and he put the phone away feeling both warmed and slightly surveilled.

Mr. Nowak turned out to be a compact man in a cardigan, standing beside a white sedan of such an advanced age that Colin, who had come along to watch, whispered, "This car is obsolescent." Mr. Nowak heard him. "This car," he said mildly, opening the driver's door, "has survived four hundred students, two hailstorms, and a raccoon with poor judgment. It will survive you." He handed Mathis the keys, which was the moment Mathis understood that the lesson had already begun, that the waiting room had only been the antechamber and this was the actual thing.

"Seat, mirror, seatbelt," Mr. Nowak said from the passenger seat. "In that order, because the mirror is useless if you set it lying down." Mathis adjusted everything twice, and his hands on the wheel were not shaking, exactly, but were holding it the way you hold a rope over a drop. "D to go, or in this car, D for probably," Nowak said. The lot was empty except for the cones, arranged in a pattern that looked, from behind the wheel, less like a course and more like a crowd of small orange judges. He pressed the gas. The car moved. It moved the way a large animal moves when it decides to cooperate, and Mathis laughed once, out of surprise, and steered around the first cone with a margin he could have parked a second car in.

They did laps of the lot while Nowak narrated in a voice like a nature documentary. "Notice how you look at the cone you're avoiding. Look where you want to go instead. The hands follow the eyes, not the other way round." It worked, which annoyed Mathis, because it meant the cones had been right and his eyes had been the problem all along. Through the window Colin gave him a thumbs up and mouthed something that was either "smooth" or "moon," and Natalie took a photograph, presumably for posterity, presumably for the group chat, presumably captioned.

On the third lap Nowak let him out onto the access road behind the building, a real road with a real speed limit, and Mathis drove at thirty kilometers an hour in a silence that had stopped being fear and become concentration. The poster was still in his head, its arithmetic sitting there, three times, per mile. He could not decide whether it was a fact about brains or a fact about statistics, whether it said something about him or only about a category he happened to fall into, and he noticed that he was doing the thing he did in essays, holding two arguments at arm's length, refusing to pick. Nowak watched the road, not him. "You're allowed to enjoy this," Nowak said. "It's not a test yet."

"It kind of feels like a test," Mathis said. "There's a poster in the waiting room that says people my age die in crashes three times as often as everyone else, per mile." Nowak hummed. "And you're out here anyway," he said. Mathis let that sit while the access road unspooled, the cones shrinking behind them, this strange brief interregnum between being driven and driving himself, and he realized he could not answer whether the poster had made him more careful or only more afraid, and that for now both of those were, apparently, driving the car. The speedometer touched forty. "There you go," Nowak said, and tapped the dash twice, gently, like patting a horse.

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: When a candidate's lead is smaller than the margin of error, the poll cannot say with confidence who is ahead, but that does not mean the race is exactly tied.
story:
Jared had taped the poll to the whiteboard before anyone else arrived, and by the time Zoey sat down he and Reuben were already leaning over it, close enough to fog the laminate. The numbers came from a survey they had run last week for Mr. Kobayashi's statistics unit, a mock election for student council president with the whole grade as their population. Alvarez had forty-four percent. Chen had forty-one percent. Beneath the figures, in Mr. Kobayashi's small neat hand, sat a line Zoey had read three times without understanding: margin of error, plus or minus five points.

"Three-point lead," Jared said, tapping the gap between the names. "Alvarez wins. That's the story. Print it."

"It's inside the margin," Reuben said. He said it the way he said most things, nonchalant, thumbs hooked in his pockets, as if the argument were already beneath him. "Three is smaller than five. So it's a tie. You can't print a winner."

"It's not a tie. Look at the numbers."

"Look at the margin."

Zoey unzipped her bag slowly and took out her notebook, because the argument had snagged on something in her and she wanted to move before it slipped away. The classroom smelled of dry-erase marker and the leftover pastries from the morning staff meeting; Reuben, who was a genuine gourmand and had once eaten four of the department's doughnuts before first bell, had already positioned himself near the box. She ignored him and copied both percentages onto a fresh page, then the margin, then drew a line under everything and stared at it.

Mr. Kobayashi was at his desk grading, and he did not look up, which Zoey had learned was deliberate with him. He wanted you to come to him. She went anyway, notebook open, and asked only whether he would tell them if they got it wrong.

"I'll tell you if you ask the right question," he said, and turned back to his grading.

She stood there a moment, feeling the answer circle somewhere just out of reach. Back at the whiteboard, Jared had begun to sketch a flyer, block letters, ALVAREZ LEADS, and Reuben was taunting him with the word tie, tie, tie, chanted under his breath the way you would at a free throw. Zoey knew that if she didn't speak now, the flyer would exist by Friday and both of them would externalize the argument into the whole hallway, posters on the trophy case, kids repeating a claim nobody had checked.

"Neither of you is right," she said.

They both turned. Her mouth was dry, which annoyed her, but she kept going. "Jared, the lead is smaller than the margin, so the poll can't say with confidence who's ahead. That part Reuben has. But that doesn't mean the race is exactly tied." She pointed at the numbers, then at the margin line, making her hand trace it so they had to watch. "It means the poll can't tell. There's a difference between can't tell and it's even. Forty-four and forty-one is what we measured. The measurement just isn't sharp enough to settle first place."

"A tie means even," Reuben said.

"No. Within the margin means unknown." She heard her own voice steady on the word and realized, with a small private jolt, that she had not been sure of this thirty seconds ago. She had assembled it at Mr. Kobayashi's desk out of the two of them, Jared's certainty and Reuben's shrug, and it had clicked only when she said it aloud. What she still didn't know, and said so, was what a bigger sample would have done to the margin, whether five points was a lot or a little, whether their two hundred respondents had been enough for anything. She wrote "uncertain" in her notebook and underlined it twice.

Jared looked at his half-finished flyer for a long moment, then crumpled the sketch and dropped it in the bin. "So what do we print?"

Zoey picked up the marker, crossed out ALVAREZ LEADS, and wrote above it: TOO CLOSE TO CALL, POLL CAN'T CONFIRM A LEADER. Reuben read it, frowned, and started to say something about a tie again, then stopped himself, chewing the inside of his cheek. From his desk, without turning, Mr. Kobayashi said, "Now that's the right question," and put down his red pen.

At the door, Reuben paused beside the pastry box, took the last doughnut, and held it out to Zoey. "Split it?"

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: Simple interest is calculated as I = P times r times t: the principal, times the annual interest rate, times the time in years.
story:
The dealership smelled like coffee burnt down to sludge and new vinyl, and Lauren stood beside a silver hatchback with one finger resting on the window sticker while her mother talked numbers with a salesman on the other side of the glass. The sticker said $11,400. Below the price, in smaller print, was a line about financing available, approved in minutes, and Lauren kept returning to that line the way her tongue returned to a loose filling.

She had four thousand saved from three summers of scooping ice cream, and her uncle had offered two thousand more, not as a gift. "I'll charge you interest," he'd said on the phone last night, fork clinking somewhere in the background. "That's the deal. You should learn what money costs."

"Interest" was the word that had followed her into the shower and onto the bus and now into this lot with its flags snapping in the March wind. Her savings account earned interest too, something small, two percent, and until this week she had thought of the word as a vague kindness the bank did her. Her uncle's version sounded more like weather.

Finlay was already there, leaning against the hatchback's hood with his arms crossed, because Finlay's family bought cars the way other families bought bread. "You're overthinking it," he said. "Everyone borrows. Nobody does the math."

"That's exactly why I want to do the math."

Inside, the salesman slid a sheet across the desk: five years, seven percent. Her mother read it with her lips pressed flat. Kelly-Anne, who had come along for the free popcorn, leaned over Lauren's shoulder and whispered, "Seven percent of what, though. Of the whole price? Every year? Is it on the four hundred you'd owe, or the eleven thousand?" Nobody answered her. The popcorn went soft in her hand.

That night, at the kitchen table with a legal pad, Lauren called her uncle back and made him say the terms twice. Simple interest, he called it. Then she wrote it out the way he'd said it: principal times the annual interest rate times the time in years. Two thousand times zero point zero five times two. She did it twice to be sure, then a third time in pen. Two hundred dollars. Borrow two thousand, pay back two thousand two hundred, if she took two years. She sat back and looked at the number, this small and definite thing, and thought about the salesman's five years and seven percent sitting somewhere under a different kind of interest she hadn't learned yet, the kind that Finlay's older brother called "how they get you."

Her mother came through with a laundry basket on her hip and read the pad upside down. "Two hundred," Lauren said. "For two years. That's the whole cost, in the open, before I sign anything." Her mother set the basket down. "My father never did this math," she said. "He signed what they put in front of him." She picked the basket up again and carried it upstairs, which for her mother was a standing ovation.

The next afternoon they went back, and Lauren asked the salesman, in front of her mother, whether the dealership's interest was simple or not. He smiled the way a person smiles at a dog that has learned to shake. "It's compounded monthly," he said, and when Kelly-Anne asked what that meant, he said it meant the interest earns interest, "which works for you when you're saving, believe me." Kelly-Anne mouthed wait, savings grow like that? and Lauren thought of her own account, her small deposits quietly doubling their small efforts, and felt an odd vertigo, the same machinery turning in two directions.

She didn't buy the car that day. She put the four thousand into an account the banker described without smiling, and her uncle's two thousand came through as a bank transfer with "SIMPLE INTEREST, YOU KNOW THE TERMS" in the memo line, which was the most affectionate thing he'd ever written her. Finlay told her she was throwing away her last teenage summer for the sake of two hundred dollars. "You could monetize the car," he said. "Deliveries, ferrying Kelly-Anne to her job for gas money." Kelly-Anne elbowed him and said being charged for rides by your friend was an externality he was imposing on her, and the two of them argued about the word until the bell over the ice cream shop door rang and Lauren had to clock in.

She kept the pad. On the back of it, in pencil, she'd written a note to herself about the salesman's kind of interest, the compounding kind, because she intended to find out exactly what five years of it did to a price and she didn't yet know. There was also the question she couldn't get straight: whether patience was really a virtue or just what people with money told people without it. The vestigial little calculator keychain her grandfather had left her sat next to the pad on her nightstand, its solar strip dead, and she pressed its buttons anyway, out of habit, two thousand, times, point zero five, times, two.

"Two hundred," she said out loud, to the empty room, and clicked the keychain off.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: The US Bill Emerson Good Samaritan Food Donation Act of 1996 gives food donors limited protection from liability, which encourages stores and restaurants to donate surplus food.
story:
The knife went through the bread faster than Jayden expected, and he almost took a knuckle with it. "Smaller," said the woman from the church group, already turning away. "They want sandwiches, not doorsteps." He cut again, more carefully, and stacked the slices on the tray. Across the basement room of St. Brendan's, the line had already formed, folding back on itself twice, and it wasn't even five o'clock.

Mr. Weiss had driven him here. His history teacher had a habit of collecting students the way other men collected stamps, and when Jayden mentioned he needed service hours for his college applications, Mr. Weiss had simply said, "Tuesday, four thirty, wear shoes you don't like." That had been the entire pitch. Now Mr. Weiss was at the sink, scrubbing industrial pots with his sleeves rolled up, looking entirely unbothered by the steam, and Jayden understood that he had been recruited for something his teacher considered ordinary.

"Bread's here," Ryden called from the stairs. Ryden had volunteered for the same reason Jayden had, more or less, except Ryden said his out loud and often: it looked good, and nobody could prove otherwise. He came down carrying four paper bags stamped with the logo of Marisol's, the Peruvian place on Fourth Street. The smell arrived before he set them down, warm and yeasted, and the woman from the church group seized two bags immediately and began loading the slicing table.

The third bag had a problem. Jayden opened it and found the rolls crushed, some of them split, a few stuck to the paper. He held one up. "These are kind of wrecked."

"So tear them up for the soup," the woman said, not looking.

"They're not moldy. They're just ugly." He turned one over in his hand. "We're throwing away food because it looks bad?"

"We're not throwing anything away. Tear them up."

He demurred, setting the bag aside instead, and carried it up the stairs to where Mr. Weiss was stacking trays. "Can we ask Marisol's for the rolls that aren't crushed? They'd probably give us fresh ones if we asked tonight."

"You want to go ask?"

"You drive."

Mr. Weiss dried his hands, which Jayden took for a yes.

Marisol herself was behind the counter, counting out change, when they came in. She recognized the bags before Jayden finished his sentence. "The bottom bag," she said. "I told the driver. The bottom bag always gets ruined." She was already moving toward the kitchen, and she talked while she worked, pulling sheet pans of bread from the warming rack. "People think I'm careless with what I send you. I'm not. I send it because I can."

Jayden didn't follow that, and said so.

"The law," she said, sliding loaves into a clean bag. "The Bill Emerson Good Samaritan Food Donation Act, 1996. It gives food donors limited protection from liability. Limited. Not total. But enough that I don't lie awake wondering if a roll will ruin me." She handed him the bag. "Before that, my mother's generation, restaurants poured bleach on the food before it went in the trash. So nobody could sue them for taking it out of the dumpster. You're too young to remember that."

He wasn't too young to be horrified by it. On the drive back he sat with the warm bag on his knees and thought about bleached bread, about a law most people had never heard of quietly deciding how many sandwiches existed in the world. In Mr. Weiss's class they had a word for this, metonymy, where a thing stands for the system that made it: the crushed rolls in the bottom bag standing for everything that got thrown away out of fear. He wasn't sure he was using it right, and he didn't ask.

The line was longer when they got back, and a man near the front had gone belligerent about the wait, loud, jabbing his finger at the serving counter, one of the other volunteers backing away from him with her ladle still in hand. Ryden was frozen at the sandwich station. Jayden set down the bread, walked the length of the table, and put a full plate in front of the man without a word. The man looked at the plate, then at Jayden, and sat.

Jayden went back to slicing. The knife moved. The bread kept coming up the stairs.

Later, sweeping, Ryden said, "So did we do good today, or did we just feel good?"

"I don't know," Jayden said. "Both, maybe. Marisol can donate because of a law. The guy yelling was hungry and angry and those aren't different things." He leaned the broom against the wall. "It helped. It didn't fix anything."

Mr. Weiss came over and took the broom out of his hand. "Wednesday, four thirty," he said. "Wear the same shoes."

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: The US National Safety Council recommends a following distance of at least three seconds, adding a second for each difficulty such as bad weather or heavy traffic.
story:
Megan's father had taped a paper cup to the dashboard of the Civic and told her that when the car ahead passed a mailbox, she should count until the cup, which was nonsense, so she was already not trusting him. It was Saturday morning in the driveway, the car still cold, and Kailey was sitting on the curb with a slushie at ten in the morning, offering commentary.

"Two seconds," Kailey said, through the straw. "That's what my cousin does. Three is for grandmas."

Her father said nothing. He had the stoic patience of a man who had already survived teaching her brother, and he folded his hands over the instruction manual on his lap like a hymnal. Megan started the car, checked the mirror out of pure ceremony, and backed down the driveway at a speed that would not have alarmed a jogger.

The neighborhood streets were wide and forgiving. She stalled twice at the same stop sign, and a man in a bathrobe walked his dog around them with the truculent air of someone who had seen many teenage drivers and rated them all poorly. Kailey honked from the curb, once, though she was not in the car and had no horn, which meant she had made the noise with her mouth.

On the straight stretch past the elementary school, her father said, "Pick a point. A pole, a shadow. When the car ahead passes it, count one thousand one, one thousand two, one thousand three."

"The National Safety Council says three seconds," he said. "At least three. And you add a second for each difficulty. Rain, heavy traffic, anything."

"So four in the rain," Megan said.

"At least."

She tried it. The car ahead was a landscaping truck with a trailer of mowers, and she counted past the fire hydrant, one two three, and it felt enormous, the gap, a whole ocean of asphalt opening up, and then a silver sedan slid into it from a side street without signaling, and she had to brake, and the counting started over. "It's not fair," she said. "Somebody takes the gap."

"Then they're the one at two seconds," her father said. "Let them."

This struck Megan as abrogating the whole project. If the rule was three seconds and everyone else on the road had voted otherwise with their bumpers, then the rule was a private religion, practiced alone, and she said so. Her father said that was true of most rules, and she could see him retreating into philosophy, which he did when he was losing, so she dropped it and counted again.

Kailey texted her a video of a guy drifting a car around a parking lot, captioned "goals." Megan, waiting at a light, watched the wheels slide sideways across the painted lines and felt two things at once: a pull toward the ease of it, the two-second life, the car as an extension of a shrug, and a smaller, quieter conviction that the counting was not cowardice but a kind of attention. Her grandmother, who had driven forty years without a single accident, had been a counter. Megan had ridden in the back seat and heard her, murmuring under her breath at every hydrant, every shadow.

The light changed. She turned left, wide and slow, and her father gripped the handle above the door but said nothing, which she appreciated. On the way home it began to rain, the first fat drops slapping the windshield and smearing into commas.

"Four seconds now," Megan said, before he could.

"Good," he said, and then, because it was raining harder, "five would be better. Traffic's getting heavy."

She counted the church steeple, the bus bench, the crosswalk sign, and let the gap stretch out in front of her while the wipers kept their patient time. A car behind her honked and swung around, close enough that she could see the driver's jaw, set and furious. Kailey was still on the curb when they pulled into the driveway, and she raised her slushie in salute.

"Still doing three?" Kailey called.

"Four," Megan said, and put the car in park, and turned off the engine, and sat for a moment with her hands still at ten and two.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: The word 'mortgage' comes from Old French for 'dead pledge', because the pledge ends either when the debt is paid or when the property is forfeited.
story:
Gabrielle sat at the kitchen table with her laptop open to three apartment listings and her grandmother's calculator, the kind with oversized buttons that clicked like tiny doors. The rent for a two-bedroom near Haylee's college was $1,650 a month, which sounded manageable until she multiplied it by twelve and then by four years and watched the number grow teeth.

"You're doing the face," her grandmother said, setting down a mug of tea that smelled of mint and burnt toast because she never believed in setting the kettle below full blast. "The face you make at crossword clues."

"The face I make at money." Gabrielle turned the laptop so her grandmother could see the listings. "Haylee and I found this place, but they want first and last month's rent up front, plus a security deposit. That's like five thousand dollars before we even own a fork."

"Deposits you get back, mostly, if you don't burn the place down." Her grandmother settled into the chair across from her, the one with the cushion that had lost its argument with gravity years ago. "Landlords aren't villains, love, whatever the internet says. They're just people who bought the house before you could."

"That's a very generous reading of some people."

"I've had generous and I've had terrible. My first landlord would pathologize any complaint. Ask about the broken radiator and suddenly you were a difficult tenant, a problematic personality." She sipped her tea. "The last one, Mr. Alvarez, he was mercurial, moods like weather, but when the pipes burst he came himself at two in the morning with a wrench and apologized to the ceiling."

Gabrielle laughed and wrote "DEPOSIT: refundable?" in her notebook. Then she paused. "Can I ask you something dumb?"

"Those are my favorite kind."

"Why is it called a mortgage? It's such a grim word. Like a mortuary with extra steps."

Her grandmother set the mug down with a click. "It isn't dumb at all. It comes from Old French. It means dead pledge."

"Dead pledge," Gabrielle repeated, and the words sat on the table between them like something from a spellbook. "That's the most metal thing I've ever heard at this table, and you once described your hip surgery."

"The pledge dies either way. Either you pay off the debt and it's over, or you can't pay and the property is forfeit. Either way, the pledge ends up dead."

"That's the opposite of what a word should do. It should get happier as you go." Gabrielle pulled the calculator toward her and started a new column. Down payment, she'd learned from a panicked midnight search, was money you put down upfront on a house you were buying, and it was enormous, like twenty percent enormous, and her savings from two summers at the garden center amounted to a rounding error of that. But rent, she was realizing, was a dead pledge too, in its own way: money paid, money gone, nothing to show at the end but four years of living somewhere.

Kristen had texted her that morning: just get the apartment, we're young, worrying about buying a house at 17 is insane. And Haylee had texted the opposite: rent is throwing money away, my cousin says so, my cousin who is twenty-two and knows everything suddenly. Gabrielle had read both messages and felt like a judge with no law book.

"Here's what nobody tells you," her grandmother said, peeling an orange with her thumbnail in one long spiral, the citrus sharp in the small kitchen. "Your grandfather and I, we rented for eleven years first. Everyone acts like renting is a character flaw. It isn't. It's what you do while you're becoming whoever's going to make the payments."

"I keep feeling like there's a right answer," Gabrielle said. "Like the adults know it and they're just waiting for me to guess."

"If we knew it, love, we'd sell it in boxes." Her grandmother dropped a section of orange into Gabrielle's palm without being asked. "You know what I think? I think you should take the apartment, and I think you should stop pretending that means you've decided anything forever."

Gabrielle looked at the orange, then at her notebook, where "DEPOSIT: refundable?" now had a star next to it and "ASK ABOUT RADIATOR" underneath. She picked up her phone and typed to both Kristen and Haylee at once: taking the place, visiting Saturday, someone bring a fork.

Then, because it felt right, she wrote one more word at the top of the page, small, in the margin where it could stay without deciding anything: mortgage.

"Can I keep the calculator?" she asked.

Her grandmother pushed it across the table, buttons clicking under her thumb, and went to yell at the kettle.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: Minnesota's Department of Transportation says the zipper merge, using both lanes up to the merge point and then taking turns, can cut a backup's length by as much as 40 percent.
story:
Carson had told everyone he failed the road test only because of parallel parking, and he told it at the bus stop that morning with enough conviction that he almost believed it himself. The truth, which he kept folded away like a receipt he didn't want to read, was that he had also panicked on the highway entrance, slowing to a crawl while a semi bore down on him, and the examiner had gripped the door handle in a way Carson chose not to remember. Still, the parallel parking version was nearly true. Nearly true counted.

Tanisha sat down beside him with a paper bag from the bakery, and the smell of butter and almond filled the shelter like she had brought it on purpose. She was a gourmand about breakfast the way other people were about dinner; she had opinions about croissants, about which corner store sold real baguettes, and she offered him half of everything before he asked. "Test's Thursday," Carson said. "Dad's letting me take the car tonight, the empty lot behind Buchanan's church. You want to come?"

"You failed parking," she said, not unkindly.

"Basically," said Carson, which was, he felt, an honest word, and also a load-bearing lie.

Emanuel drove them after school in his cosmopolitan hand-me-down sedan, the one with a radar detector and a bobblehead and stickers from three countries Carson couldn't identify, and he positioned cones in the church lot while Carson practised until the streetlights came on. He got it right four times in a row and wrong twice, and Emanuel expostulated from the curb at the fifth attempt, "You're not turning the wheel till your bumper's past their taillight, man, that's the whole thing," and on the sixth try the tires kissed the curb so gently it felt like the car had decided to be good on its own.

The highway part they saved for Thursday morning, the actual test route, because the DOT had closed one lane past the bridge for construction. Carson's father rode in back, silent, doing the crossword. Traffic slowed near the cones, and the right lane, the one ending ahead, stood nearly empty while their lane crawled. Carson signalled and edged over immediately, early, feeling righteous, and a white pickup shot past them in the open lane and cut in at the front, and Carson's father looked up from the crossword and said only, "Huh."

"Jerk," Carson said.

"They're called zipper merges," his father said, and went back to five across. That was all he said. That was all he ever said about anything.

Carson stewed about it through the test, which he took and passed, parking included, his hands steady even though his mind was two exits back on the highway. Afterward he sat at the bus stop outside the DMV, licence in his wallet, waiting for the 42 because his father had driven the car to work and being licensed, he discovered, changed nothing about a Tuesday. Tanisha found him there on her way home. "You passed," she said, reading his face before he said a word.

"I merged early," he said. "The whole way, both times. It felt polite." He told her about the pickup, and about his father's single syllable, and then, because Emanuel had texted him a link while he waited, he showed her his phone. Minnesota's Department of Transportation said the zipper merge, using both lanes up to the merge point and then taking turns, could cut a backup's length by as much as 40 percent. He'd read it twice. It felt backwards to him, like being told the rude thing was the right thing, and he said so.

"So you're going to drive up a closing lane with your blinker on like you own it," Tanisha said.

"I don't know," Carson said. "Maybe I ease in. Maybe I take my turn and let one car in ahead of me, exactly one, like teeth." He watched the traffic on the avenue, two lanes folding into one near the utility work, drivers who had all decided, each of them, whether to be polite or efficient, none of them agreeing. He had passed the test and that was supposed to be the finish line, and instead here was a new thing he was only starting to hold: that the rules of the road and the rules of consideration weren't always the same rules, and that he'd have to choose, every merge, which one he was following.

The 42 came around the corner, and Tanisha stood, then paused, one hand on the pole. "First ride on your licence," she said. "Or are you practising something?"

Carson looked at the bus, then down the street toward the lot behind Buchanan's church, where the cones would still be standing in the dark. "Walk with me," he said.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Edmund Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France, published in 1790, condemned the Revolution for destroying tradition, and set the conservative view that historians after 1800 argued with.
story:
The rain had followed them from the bus stop, and by the time Alexandra, Joel, and Claudia reached the door of the old library attached to the Hartwell House museum, her draft essay was damp at the corners where it stuck out of her bag. Seven pages on how historians had judged the French Revolution, and every page argued the same thing, that scholars after 1800 lined up against the violence, one dry voice after another. Ms. Choi, the archivist, had agreed to let them work in the reading room before the museum opened, but only if they touched nothing without gloves.

"It's not an argument if everyone agrees with you," Claudia said, peeling off her wet coat. "That's a parade."

"I don't have time for a parade and an essay." Alexandra spread the draft on the long oak table. The room smelled of cold stone and old paper, and beneath the window a display case held a row of leather bindings with their spines turned outward, too far away to read. She had chosen the topic herself three weeks ago, mostly because it had sounded impressive on the form, and now the essay was due Monday and she still did not know what her own position was. Every time she tried to write a conclusion, it dissolved into a list.

Joel leaned over her pages, chewing the end of a pen. "So all these people writing after 1800, they're just arguing with the Revolution itself? With something that happened?"

"Obviously."

"It doesn't seem obvious." He tapped the margin. "People usually argue with other people, not with events."

Ms. Choi came in with a trolley of document boxes, and Alexandra asked, carefully, keeping it casual, whether the library had anything on how views of the Revolution had changed. Ms. Choi said the collection held a few relevant items, and that if Alexandra wanted to see the case at the window she was welcome to look, provided she kept her hands behind her back. Then she left them alone with the boxes, and Alexandra, who had been awake since five, felt the first faint unease that her seven pages were not a foundation but a wall around an empty lot.

She crossed to the case. The bindings were cracked and dark, and the card beside them gave dates and titles in faded ink. She read down the list, and her eyes snagged, then stopped. One entry was earlier than all the rest. She stood very still while Joel and Claudia argued behind her about whether pragmatics mattered in an essay about history, whether you had to ask not only what historians wrote but what they thought they were doing when they wrote it. She was not listening anymore. The card in front of her read: Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, 1790.

"Joel. Come here."

He came. He read the card twice. "That's before 1800. Your whole essay starts after 1800."

"I know when it starts." But the essay was not all she was thinking about. She was thinking that she had seen the name before, in a footnote she had skipped, in a book she had skimmed in the school library because the print was small. She had assumed a book that old could not matter, that the argument she was tracing had begun with the historians, not before them. The case glass held her reflection, faint and doubled over the old binding.

Ms. Choi returned with the gloves. "You found it," she said, not a question, and offered to open the case so they could see the title page properly. Her gloved hands eased the book onto a foam rest, and Alexandra bent close. She did not touch it. On the walk back from the bus she had been drafting a new opening paragraph in her head, something embryonic, half argument and half guess, about a tradition of disagreement, but she had not known where it began.

She read what was visible of the title page, then straightened. "So this condemned it. The Revolution. For destroying tradition." She said it slowly, testing it.

"That's the conservative view," Joel said, reading over her shoulder. "Your historians after 1800, that's what they were arguing with. Not the event. Him."

Alexandra sat back down at the table and pulled the draft toward her. The first seven pages were wrong, or at least wrong enough that honesty required her to say so, out loud, to the room. She took out a pen and drew a single line through her old opening, then turned to a fresh page. Claudia slid the document box closer without being asked, and the rain went on against the tall windows.

"Start with a book nobody asked you to start with," Claudia said.

Alexandra wrote the date, 1790, and then, beneath it, one sentence that did not yet know where it was going.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: In a LEFT JOIN, putting a condition on the right table in the WHERE clause, like orders.total > 0, removes the NULL rows and makes it act like an inner join.
story:
Isabella had promised her mother she would stay quiet in the corner cubicle, but the database on the screen was louder than any office could be. For an hour she had been teaching herself SQL from a book with a cracked spine, working through the sample data her mother had copied onto a spare laptop: customers in one table, orders in another, a small archipelago of rectangles on the whiteboard she had claimed as her own.

Her mother's colleague had given her a real task, half as a joke. Find the customers who never ordered anything, he had said, and Isabella had taken it as a summons. She drew the two tables out on the whiteboard, connected them with a line, and wrote her first query, a LEFT JOIN that kept every customer whether or not they had orders. She ran it. There was Mrs. Okonkwo with her four purchases, there was the bakery with eleven, and there, at the bottom, were the rows she wanted: customers with nothing beside their names, the join leaving empty spaces where their orders should have been.

She was still pleased with herself when Lea-Rose texted a screenshot of her own homework, which looked suspiciously similar, and then Colby arrived to be dropped off for a ride home later and pulled a second chair up beside her. "Show me the ghost customers," he said, and Isabella ran the query again so he could see the blank columns, the customers who ordered nothing.

Then she spoiled it. She wanted the list cleaner, so she added a filter in the WHERE clause, orders.total > 0, to keep only positive totals, and ran it again. The ghosts were gone. Every single customer with no orders had vanished from the result, and what remained was the ordinary list of people who had bought things. She sat back and stared. "Where did they go?" Colby asked, and Isabella said, "I don't know. That's the problem."

She tried it with the filter removed, and the ghosts returned. She added it, and they left again, obedient to something she could not see. It was as if the join were two different joins depending on where she put her condition. She rubbed her eyes, wondering whether the machine was inconsistent, and then wondering, more honestly, whether she was the one being inconsistent, whether she had assumed a rule without ever testing it.

"What did you change between the runs?" Lea-Rose asked over video call, her face small in the corner of the screen, and Isabella explained the filter, orders.total greater than zero, sitting in the WHERE clause. "Try moving it somewhere else," Lea-Rose suggested, and Colby, who had been reading the book's chapter on joins, tapped a paragraph. Isabella tried placing the condition inside the join itself instead of in the WHERE clause, and the ghosts survived the filter this time. The customers with no orders stayed in the list.

"So the WHERE clause is doing something to the empties," Colby said slowly. Isabella nodded, copying the sentence into her notebook in her own handwriting, the way she kept things she did not yet fully trust. With the condition on the right table in the WHERE clause, the rows with nothing in them were being removed, and the join stopped behaving the way it had before. She underlined it twice. "It acted like an inner join," she said, and Colby repeated the words back to her, trying the shape of them.

Her mother's colleague, passing with a coffee, glanced at her screen and asked if she had proselytized yet, converted any of the disaffected accountants to the church of proper queries. Isabella laughed and said not yet. She looked at her two working queries side by side, one that kept the customers who ordered nothing and one that had quietly discarded them, and she could not say which had surprised her more: that the machine was so literal, or that she had spent an hour believing she understood something she had only memorized. She printed both results, wrote LEFT JOIN and WHERE in the margin of each, and pinned them side by side on the whiteboard among her rectangles.

"I still don't know why it happens," she told Colby, and he shrugged and said maybe that was next week. Isabella pulled the laptop closer, deleted her filter, and typed it again, one letter at a time, watching the ghost rows appear.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: English newspaper headlines often drop small words like 'the' and use the present tense for past events, a compressed style sometimes called 'headlinese'.
story:
The festival had taken over the whole park by noon, and Avery could smell the grill smoke from the Greek booth before she found her nametag. Mr. Papadopoulos handed her a stack of photocopied articles along with her volunteer sticker. "Read one, then tell me what it says, in your own words, out loud," he said. "That is the whole task. The newspaper stand is part of the heritage exhibit." He tapped the top page, a short item about a local library reopening, and left her to it.

She carried the paper to a folding chair near the stage, where Rafael was untangling a string of lights. Three months in the country and she could order food, apologize, describe the weather, but a newspaper still looked to her like a wall with the mortar knocked out. The headline was the worst of it: COUNCIL REOPENS LIBRARY AFTER FLOOD. She read it four times and felt her face go warm. Where were the little words? In her own language, the sentence would have needed its small connective syllables the way a necklace needs thread. This had none, and it used the present tense for something that had already happened, as though the council were reopening the library at this very moment, in the park, between the grill and the bouncy castle.

"It's like it has no grammar at all," she said to Rafael, who had given up on the lights and sat down beside her.

He leaned over the page. "Headlinese," he said. "My cousin calls it that. They drop the small words and use the present for past stuff. Gets more in."

"The present for the past," Avery repeated. That was the mortar, then, or a different kind of mortar, one she had never been taught. It was not that the language had failed her; it was that it had a second, compressed register she had walked past a hundred times on bus shelters and corner boxes without knowing she was reading anything at all.

Thalie arrived with two paper cups of lemonade and peered at the article over Avery's shoulder. "So what does it say? Summarize it."

Avery hesitated. The old instinct was to translate word by word and hope the sentence assembled itself, the way she had done in her first weeks, standing at a bus stop, asking a stranger for directions and receiving a torrent she could only nod at. That stranger had probably thought her rude. She had gone home and felt a visceral shame, the kind that lives in the stomach rather than the head, and had nearly quit the evening class. Instead she had made a rule for herself: never fake understanding, never guess at the shape of a thing and present the guess as knowledge. Her grandmother had an aphorism about this, something about how a borrowed axe cuts crooked, and Avery had repeated it so often it had become almost a superstition.

She set the cup down without drinking. "In May there was a flood," she said slowly. "The library closed. Now the council has opened it again, and there will be a small ceremony on Saturday." She listened to herself as though to a stranger. Each fact was in the past where it belonged, held together with the small words she had missed in the headline. It was not a translation of the headline; it was a summary of the article, which was the actual task, and she had nearly let a compressed style impugn her confidence in her own reading when the problem was never her grammar at all.

"Perfect," Thalie said. "Boring, but perfect."

Mr. Papadopoulos came back with a tray of pastries and stood listening without saying anything, the way he did. Avery realized she was still holding the article and that her hands had stopped trembling somewhere in the middle of the second sentence. But a question remained, and she turned it over while the loudspeaker announced the folk dancers. The compression worked for natives, presumably; it saved space; it had its own logic. What she could not yet decide was whether she should learn to write that way too, to fold herself into the shorthand of this new place, or whether keeping her full sentences, all that careful mortar, was the better part of who she was becoming. Both felt true. She looked at the headline again, then at the stage where the dancers were taking their places.

"Next one," she said, and pulled the second article from the stack.

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: In the balanced equation 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, two moles of hydrogen gas react with one mole of oxygen gas to form two moles of water.
story:
The garage smelled of motor oil and the cold that crept under the door, and Nevaeh sat on an upturned milk crate with her chemistry book open across her knees. Her father's workbench held the flashlight she was supposed to be fetching an hour ago, but the retake exam was on Thursday, and she had already failed the unit once. Lucas sat on the concrete beside her, spinning a socket wrench like a lazy wheel.

"You're doing the thing again," he said. "The staring-at-the-page thing."

"I'm thinking."

"You're stalling." He set the wrench down. "Okay. Start from the top. What's the question even asking?"

She read it aloud, her voice flat. "What mass of water forms when four grams of hydrogen gas reacts completely with oxygen?" The numbers sat there like a locked gate. "I know the balanced equation. I wrote it out. Two H two plus O two gives two H two O."

Lucas leaned over and looked at her notebook, where she had drawn the equation twice, the second time with little tally marks under each molecule. "So count them," he said. "You told me Ms. Santoso makes you count atoms."

"That's for little kids."

"You failed the test, so maybe don't be snobby about it." He tapped her tallies with the pen. "Left side. How many hydrogens?"

She counted, feeling stupid and doing it anyway. "Four. Two molecules, two atoms each. Then the oxygen molecule has two atoms." She moved her finger across. "Right side, two water molecules. Two hydrogens each is four, one oxygen each is two. It matches."

"So two moles of hydrogen gas react with one mole of oxygen gas," Lucas said, reading off her own margin note, "and you get two moles of water. That's what your equation says."

"It sounds bombastic when you say it like that."

"It sounds like math." He grinned. "Now the four grams. That's where you were stuck?"

Nevaeh flipped back to the table of molar masses. "Hydrogen gas is about two grams per mole. So four grams of it is two moles." She wrote it down, and then the gate opened almost on its own: two moles of hydrogen meant two moles of water, and water was eighteen grams per mole, so thirty-six grams. She checked it twice. Thirty-six.

"That's it?" she said. "That's the whole unit?"

"The whole unit is converting between grams and moles and back, over and over, until you stop being scared of the word."

"It's not the word." She paused. "Okay, it's a little the word. Moles. Who looked at a chemical amount and thought of a squinting rodent."

"Some chemist probably loved the pun. You'd know if you'd done the reading on the history of it."

"Mr. Pontificate," she said, and threw a wood shaving at him.

He caught it. "You know what's funny, though? In your equation, all the hydrogen becomes water. Every atom you started with shows up on the other side. Nothing's lost."

"Conservation of mass." She said it the way Ms. Santoso said it, half a question. The garage ticked as the cold metal outside contracted. Nevaeh looked at the equation again, at her tallies, and thought of her father in this same garage the summer before he left, rebuilding a carburetor with parts laid out in labeled rows, everything accounted for, nothing vanished. She had believed, for most of a year, that people could just disappear. It was strange to think that even the strictest bookkeeping only worked for atoms.

"Hey," Lucas said. "Where'd you go?"

"Nowhere. My dad used to do this. Count parts so nothing got lost."

Lucas was quiet for a second, which was rare enough that she noticed. "My mom does that with receipts," he said. "Everything in its column. I used to think it was about money. Now I think it's about knowing where things went."

Nevaeh closed the notebook, then opened it again and wrote the answer in the margin, boxed it the way Ms. Santoso liked. Thirty-six grams. Two moles in, two moles out. She understood the arithmetic completely and understood nothing about the rest, and for once she let both of those be true at the same time without trying to force one to explain the other.

"Quiz me on the phonetics of it," she said. "Say a compound, I'll say the molar mass."

"Phonetics is sounds, Nevaeh. Words. That's not even the right field."

"Fine. Then say the words and I'll do the numbers. Sodium chloride."

"Wouldn't you rather know if you got it right first?"

"No. Ask me again until I stop flinching."

Lucas picked up the socket wrench, spun it once, and said, "Sodium chloride. Go."

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Without its natural greenhouse effect, Earth's average surface temperature would be about minus 18 degrees Celsius instead of roughly 14 degrees Celsius.
story:
The graph had been printed on cheap paper, and the ink was already fading where Isabella had traced it with a pencil, following the line as it bent upward after 1950 like something deciding, slowly, to leave. She had taped it to the fence between the hydrangeas and the compost bin, because her bedroom felt like a place for reverie and she wanted this to be work.
