Tomorrow she would stand up in Mr. Popescu's class and explain it, and Mr. Popescu had a way of asking one question you could not have prepared for.

Flora arrived first, carrying two glasses of iced tea without being asked, because she had noticed Isabella forget to eat on days like this. She set one on the upturned crate Isabella was using as a desk. "So teach me," Flora said, folding herself onto the grass. "I know nothing. Genuinely nothing."

Isabella pointed at the jagged red line. "This is carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, measured every year, going back about a century." The line climbed in small sawtooth steps, rising and dipping, rising and dipping, but always higher than the decade before.

"Why does it wiggle?"

"The seasons. Forests breathe." She said it and realized, as she said it, that she had never thought of the whole planet breathing before, one breath per year, and Flora was watching her have that thought instead of the answer she owed her. "Anyway. It goes up."

Dallas came through the side gate without knocking, as he had since they were nine. He had spent the spring trying to monetize a skateboarding channel and had opinions about everything, which he delivered while eating the cherries meant for all three of them. "My uncle says greenhouse gases are a scam," he said, spitting a pit into the compost. "Some natural thing the planet does anyway."

"No, that part is true," Isabella said, surprising herself. "That's the strange part. It's natural, and we depend on it."

Flora shaded her eyes. "Depend on it how?"

Here was the fact Isabella had found three nights ago, buried in a library book with a cracked spine, and she had copied it onto her palm in pen and then washed it off before anyone could see. She said it now, carefully, like carrying water in her hands. "Without its natural greenhouse effect, Earth's average surface temperature would be about minus eighteen degrees Celsius." She let that sit. "Instead of roughly fourteen."

Dallas stopped chewing. "Minus eighteen. That's, like, freezer."

"That's a frozen rock. Nothing green anywhere." Flora pulled a blade of grass and looked at it, at the small ordinary fact of its being alive, as if the number had made it newly improbable.

Dallas, though, argued as a matter of principle, and Isabella had to respect him for it, because the argument was real. "So it's good," he said. "The gases. If they keep us warm enough to live, then why is everyone saying they're bad? Which is it?"

"That's what I couldn't get past either," Isabella admitted. She tapped the graph, the sawtooth line with its patient, accelerating climb. "I kept wanting it to be one or the other. Like it had to be a villain or a hero."

"And?"

"And I think it's both, and neither. It's more like it's a thing that's good at a certain amount." She held her hands apart, a span of air between them. "The effect itself is what we live inside. But this," she pointed at the steep last stretch of the line, "this is us changing how much of it there is. The problem isn't the blanket. It's what happens when the blanket gets thicker, and that's the part I still can't explain very well, because I don't fully understand it yet." She heard Mr. Popescu's imagined question and felt the honest shape of her not-knowing. "Tomorrow, if someone asks me exactly why more carbon dioxide means more trapped heat, molecule by molecule, I'll have to say I'm still working on that."

Flora had gone quiet, drawing in the dirt with a twig. She was the one who named every plant on the street and had once explained to Isabella, at length, why the neighbor's roses had different colors, something she called phenotypic variation, the same seeds making different flowers depending on where they grew. Now she said, "So we're like the roses. Same planet, different conditions, and the conditions decide what can live here."

"That's prettier than anything I was going to say tomorrow."

"You can't say roses in a science presentation, Isabella."

"I can say it at the end. As long as the graph comes first."

Dallas gathered the cherry pits he had scattered and dropped them in the compost, an apology of sorts, since he had eaten most of them. He looked at the taped-up paper for a long moment, the sawtooth line still climbing toward the fence's top edge. "Minus eighteen," he said again, quieter this time. He picked up the iced tea Flora had saved for him and hadn't mentioned saving.

The evening came on. Somewhere down the block a sprinkler ticked its slow circle, and the hydrangeas gave off their plain green smell, and Isabella took the graph down off the fence because the dew would ruin it. She rolled it carefully and put a rubber band around it, and Flora, standing to go, straightened the crate and carried the empty glasses toward the kitchen door without being asked.

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: A 2013 study by Carl Benedikt Frey and Michael Osborne estimated that 47 percent of US jobs were at high risk of automation.
story:
The boxes arrived at Hargrove's on Tuesday, four of them shrink-wrapped on pallets, and by Thursday Emile was training the self-checkout machines, which meant standing beside them while a woman from the vendor company scanned a basket of practice items over and over until the scales agreed with the software. He was seventeen and had worked the registers for eleven months, long enough to know the regulars, the woman who bought the same yogurt every Wednesday, the man who always paid in rolled quarters, and now the store had installed four stations that did not need to know anyone at all. On Friday he came home with his name tag still pinned to his shirt and found Desirae already at the table, her laptop open beside the casserole.

"Sit," his mother said, and he sat, and the casserole went around, and Desirae turned the laptop toward him before he had finished serving himself.

"Look at this. I found it for my econ thing." She scrolled to a highlighted line and tapped the screen twice, the way she did when she wanted him to understand that a thing was important. "Read it out loud so it sticks."

He read it out loud so it would stick. "A 2013 study by Carl Benedikt Frey and Michael Osborne estimated that 47 percent of US jobs were at high risk of automation." The words sat on the dinner table next to the green beans. "Forty-seven percent," he said again, quieter, because the number wanted saying twice.

"Which jobs?" his father asked, spearing a piece of chicken. He had driven trucks for twenty-two years and had recently begun talking about a hiking trip in the fall, some trail through montane forest he had saved on his phone, photographs of fir and low cloud he showed everyone who stood still long enough.

"Mine, for a start," Emile said. "They put the machines in this week. I trained them." He described the vendor woman, her lanyard, her flat voice saying the machine learns from repetition, and how he had stood there like some kind of acolyte, ringing up practice baskets for a thing that would replace him. Desirae laughed at the word, and then stopped laughing when she saw his face.

"That's exactly why I came over, actually." She leaned forward, elbows on the table, and his mother gave the elbows a look that Desirae, absorbed, did not notice. "The coding club got a grant. Ms. Anderson is sponsoring it, and there's a summer track, app development, portfolio stuff. Colleges love it. You're better at logic problems than anyone in the class and you're wasting it on bagging groceries for people who don't say thank you."

"I like the people who say thank you," Emile said. "That's the point of the job. Some of them only talk to me all day. There's one guy, quarters guy, he asks me how school's going because nobody else asks him anything."

"You can like them and still take the class. It's not betrayal to learn the tools."

"Isn't it, though?" He heard his own voice go sharp and dialed it back. "If I learn to build the things that take the jobs, I'm just moving to the winning side and calling it a plan."

His mother set down her fork. "Emile. Don't prevaricate with us. You either want the class or you don't, but don't turn it into a speech about the world while your chicken gets cold." She said it mildly, the way she said most things, and it landed harder for that. Desirae opened her mouth and his mother raised one finger, not unkindly, and Desirae closed it.

They ate for a while. His father told them about the trail again, the elevation, the night he would spend above the treeline, and Emile listened with half an ear and thought about the machines learning from repetition. It was not that the machines were evil. They counted correctly and never called in sick, and the store's margins were thin, he knew that too, and if the machines kept prices low for the quarter man's yogurt, was that a harm or a help, and to whom. The 47 percent was a national number, an abstraction, and yet it had arrived in his store in four shrink-wrapped boxes and it would arrive everywhere else the same way, without malice, without anyone deciding anything all at once.

He thought also of Desirae, who had not come to save him but to recruit him, because she wanted a partner for the grant project and because she genuinely believed, the way she genuinely believed everything, that code was the lifeboat and the sensible climbed in. She was not wrong. He could not prove she was wrong. That was the part that kept snagging: taking the class did not require him to approve of the machines, only to stop pretending he could stand outside them.

"Okay," he said finally. "I'll come to one meeting. One. And I'm keeping the Saturday shifts until they take them."

"Deal," Desirae said, and slid the laptop back, and under the table her knee bounced the way it did when she'd won something.

After dinner he took the plates to the sink and looked out the window at the parking lot, where a line of carts waited for the boy whose job, someday, was also in that 47 percent. Then he went to his room, found Ms. Anderson's email address on the club page, and typed, "Tuesday works. Can I still ask questions that don't have answers?"

fact: TinEye, a reverse image search engine launched in 2008, can sort results with the oldest first, helping find when an image first appeared online.
story:
Carson's father had given him a key to the office years ago, back when the building still felt enormous to him, and now Saturday mornings there were a ritual: the hum of the obsolescent copier on its warm-up cycle, the vending machine on the third floor that still took dollar coins, and a desk by the window where Carson spread out his homework while his father caught up on paperwork two rooms away. He had his history essay half drafted, something about the printing press and authority, when his phone began to shudder against the desk. In the group chat, Larissa had posted a photo with no caption except three exclamation points. A highway drowned to the guardrails, brown water sliding across the asphalt, and riding the surface of it, unmistakable, a shark. Beneath the photo she had written, "This is 20 minutes from Savanah's house. Nobody go out."

Carson stared at it. The light in the photo was strange, greenish, and something in him reached for his phone to forward it to three other people before the better part of him put the phone down on the desk. His thumb hovered over the screen. His father came through with a mug of coffee and looked over his shoulder.

"Shark on the freeway," Carson said. "Larissa says it's near Savanah's."

His father made a noncommittal sound and went back to his filing. He was a man who trusted paper, who kept drawers of it, and Carson had inherited from him a suspicion of anything that arrived too perfectly. The photo was too perfect. The shark was centered. The water was photogenic. He was still turning the phone over in his hand when a message arrived from Savanah herself, a screenshot of a webpage and one line: "Not new. I checked."

Below that, a second message: "Do a reverse image search. I used a site called TinEye. It's been around since 2008, so it caught the old copies."

Carson read it twice. He had never heard of the thing, had no sense of how a search could run backward from a picture instead of from words, but the office computer was already awake in front of him, its screensaver dissolving into the spreadsheet his father had abandoned. He pulled up the site, saved Larissa's photo to the desktop, and uploaded it, feeling faintly like a forger handling stolen goods. The results took a moment. Then a column of pages appeared, dozens of them, each one the same shark, the same green water. The most recent ones were from today, from accounts screaming about the storm. And there, at the top of the list when he clicked the option to sort the oldest first, was a page dated years back, some fishing forum where somebody had posted the picture as a joke about flooded roads in another state entirely.

"Found it," he said out loud, to no one.

His father drifted over and squinted at the screen. "How'd you do that?"

"You flip the search around. You give it the picture and it finds where the picture's been." Carson pointed at the oldest result. "This photo's older than the storm."

His father nodded slowly, the way he did when the copier managed a two-sided job without jamming. "Sort of problematizes the whole idea of eyewitness sharing," he said, and wandered off with his coffee, satisfied with the sentence, unaware he had handed Carson a line for his essay.

There was still the matter of Larissa. Carson knew her well enough to know she would not like being wrong, and well enough to know she had not invented the fear. The storm was real. Savanah's street did flood, had flooded two springs ago to the porches. The shark was the lie, or not even a lie exactly, a decoration, a thing that made a real danger more vivid and therefore more shareable. He typed three drafts of a reply and deleted them all, because each one sounded like a lecture, and Larissa would hear a lecture from him as a kind of lording. In the fourth draft he pasted the link to the old forum page and added only, "The flooding's real though. Check on your street."

While he waited he clicked through the other results, out of something that was no longer urgency but curiosity, the essay part of his mind assembling itself without his permission. The same image had migrated through years of floods, hurricane seasons, monsoons in countries he couldn't place, each time freshly captioned, each time urgent. It belonged to a genus of picture, he thought, the disaster shark, the church engulfed in flames, the soldier saluting a dog, pictures that lived forever and were born again every emergency. His history teacher had spent a week on woodcuts of sea monsters sold to people who would never see the sea. He began typing that into the essay, then stopped and looked at the word he had written, uncertain whether the connection was real insight or a convenient rhyme between centuries.

Larissa's reply came as a phone call. He picked up and heard her breathing before she spoke.

"You're sure it's the same photo," she said. "Not just a similar one."

"I sorted them oldest first. The forum post is from years ago. Somebody in the comments even ID'd the shark. It's a whale shark, and the guy said it was photoshopped into a flooded road, some other flood, some other year." He paused. "Whale sharks aren't even the scary genus. They eat plankton."

There was a silence on the line, and he let her have it without filling it.

"I sent it to my aunt," Larissa said finally. "And to like six people at school."

"So send them the link."

"What do I even say?"

"Say the water's real," Carson said, "and the shark isn't." He could hear her typing already, her keyboard clattering somewhere across town, and behind him the copier finished its warm-up and began to run, sheet after sheet feeding through, printing out something neither of them would ever read.
